a: like people moaning about hard times
p: The Hebrew verb here appears only once more in the Bible. Translators guess at its exact sense.
b: The usual word for grumbling in the wilderness is lun (14:2, 27; Exodus 16:2). Here the text uses a different and rare form, mit'onenim, found elsewhere only in Lamentations 3:39 ("Why should any living person grumble?"). It may mean "to moan" or "to grieve over oneself." The KJV has "complained"; the Greek translators of the Septuagint wrote that the people "grumbled evil things." The Hebrew does not say what they moaned about. Rashi says they were looking for an excuse to turn away from God. The rest of the chapter gives the answer: the road was hard, and they wanted Egypt's food.

a: ate up the edge of the camp
p: The rabbis asked why the fire burned only the edge of the camp, and gave two answers.
b: The Sifre on Numbers offers two readings of "edge" (qetseh). One says it means the lowest people, the riffraff at the fringes, and links them with the "hangers-on" of 11:4. The other says it means the most distinguished, the "ends" or leaders, because judgment begins with those who should know better. Rashi records both. A plain reading is simpler: the fire struck the outskirts as a warning and did not sweep the whole camp, because Moses prayed (11:2). Taberah is listed among the places where Israel angered the LORD in Deuteronomy 9:22, but it is missing from the full list of stops in Numbers 33.

a: Taberah
p: Taberah means "burning." Like many places in these chapters, it is named for what happened there.
b: Numbers 11 names two places after their events: Taberah, "burning" (from ba'ar, "to burn"), and Kibroth Hattaavah, "graves of craving" (11:34). Later come Hormah, "destruction" (14:45; 21:3), and Meribah, "quarrel" (20:13). The map of the wilderness becomes a map of Israel's failures. Source critics see these as old place-name stories (etiologies), told to explain names that people still knew. Traditional readers see the names as memorials the people were meant to remember (Deuteronomy 9:22).

a: The hangers-on
p: The Hebrew word comes from "gather": a collected crowd. Jewish tradition blames them for starting the trouble.
b: The word asafsuf appears only here. It comes from asaf, "to gather," and suggests a crowd of people who had attached themselves to Israel: the KJV has "the mixt multitude." Most readers link them with the "large mixed crowd" that went up from Egypt with Israel (Exodus 12:38), non-Israelites who joined the exodus. Rashi and the Sifre say these converts started the craving, and the Israelites followed. The text does not let Israel off: "the Israelites too began to weep again." Modern readers note that the story blames the outsiders first, but it punishes everyone who craved (11:33–34).

a: were seized by a craving
p: The Hebrew doubles the word. Psalm 78 and Paul both remember this craving.
b: The Hebrew says literally "they craved a craving" (hit'avvu ta'avah). The same root names the place at the end of the chapter, Kibroth Hattaavah, "graves of the craving" (11:34). Psalm 78:18 and 78:29–31 retell the scene: God gave them what they craved, but while the food was still in their mouths his anger rose against them. Psalm 106:14–15 adds, "He gave them what they demanded, but he sent a thinning sickness down their throats." Paul uses the scene as a warning for the church: these things happened "so that we would not crave evil things, as they craved" (1 Corinthians 10:6).

a: for nothing
p: Slaves did not eat fish for free. The rabbis read "for nothing" as "free of commandments."
b: Fish from the Nile and its canals were a staple of the Egyptian poor, and cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic were common vegetables. The Greek historian Herodotus (2.125) says an inscription on the Great Pyramid recorded the cost of radishes, onions and garlic for the workers. Still, "for nothing" is the rosy memory of hungry people: they were slaves (Exodus 1:11–14). The Sifre and Rashi read the phrase another way: in Egypt they ate "free of commandments," without the burden of God's law, and that freedom is what they really missed.

a: bdellium
p: Bdellium is a pale, sweet-smelling tree resin. The only other time it appears in the Bible is in Eden.
b: Hebrew bedolach is usually identified with bdellium, a yellowish, waxy gum from a tree related to myrrh, found in Arabia and India. It appears only here and in Genesis 2:12, where it lies in the land of Havilah near Eden, with gold and onyx. The comparison gives the manna's color and sheen. Exodus 16:31 says it was "white" and tasted "like a honey wafer"; here it tastes like a cake made with oil (11:8). The Talmud harmonizes the descriptions: it tasted like bread to young men, like oil to the old, and like honey to small children (Yoma 75b). Later midrash adds that each person tasted whatever he wished.

a: the way a foster father carries a nursing baby
p: Moses pictures himself as a parent carrying a baby, and says God should be the one doing it.
b: The Hebrew omen means a guardian or foster parent; the feminine form, omenet, is a nurse (Ruth 4:16; 2 Samuel 4:4). The baby here is a "suckling," a child still nursing. Moses' point is sharp: "Did I conceive them? Did I give birth to them?" He implies that God is the one who conceived and bore this people, so God should carry them. The Bible elsewhere uses such motherly pictures of God (Deuteronomy 32:18; Isaiah 46:3–4; Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:13). Paul uses the same picture of himself as a nursing mother to the church (1 Thessalonians 2:7).
r: Deuteronomy 1:31; Deuteronomy 32:18; Isaiah 46:3–4; Isaiah 49:15; Isaiah 66:13; 1 Thessalonians 2:7

a: my own misery
p: Jewish tradition counts this phrase among a few places where scribes softened words to avoid offending God.
b: The rabbis listed some passages they called tiqqune soferim, "corrections of the scribes," places where an older reading was said to be changed out of reverence. Lists of them appear in the Mekhilta (on Exodus 15:7), the Sifre on Numbers (on 10:35) and later Masoretic notes, and the lists do not always agree. Here the tradition says Moses originally said "do not let me look on your evil" or "their evil," that is, the disaster God would bring on Israel. Most scholars think many of these "corrections" are later explanations, not real changes, since no surviving manuscript has the other reading.

a: seventy men from the elders of Israel
p: Seventy elders already stood with Moses at Sinai. Later Judaism traced its high court to them.
b: Seventy elders went up the mountain with Moses and saw the God of Israel (Exodus 24:1, 9). Here seventy are given a share of Moses' spirit to carry the people with him. This is the second time Moses gets help: in Exodus 18:21–26 Jethro advised him to appoint judges. The Mishnah says the Great Sanhedrin had seventy-one members, "since Moses was over them" (Sanhedrin 1:6). Seventy is a number of fullness, like the seventy nations of Genesis 10. Jesus sends out seventy (or seventy-two, in some manuscripts) in Luke 10:1, and the legend of the Septuagint says seventy-two elders translated the Law.

a: I will draw off some of the spirit that is on you
t: Did Moses lose some of his spirit?
p: The Hebrew verb means to set aside a portion. The rabbis said Moses lost nothing, like a candle lighting others.
b: The verb atsal means to set apart or reserve some of something. Did Moses then have less? The Sifre and Rashi answer with a famous picture: Moses was like a lamp from which other lamps are lit, and its own light does not grow less. Others read it as a real sharing of one gift among many. The same idea appears when Elisha asks for a "double share" of Elijah's spirit (2 Kings 2:9), and when Joshua receives "some of your majesty" from Moses (27:20). Christians often read the scene in light of Pentecost, when the Spirit came on many (Acts 2).

a: six hundred thousand men on foot
p: The number matches the census of chapter 1. How to read such large numbers is discussed at 1:46.
b: Moses rounds the census figure of 603,550 fighting men (1:46; Exodus 12:37). With women, children and the elderly, a traditional reading gives two million or more people, which makes Moses' question in 11:22 all the sharper. Some scholars who take the story as history read the Hebrew elef, "thousand," as a clan or military unit, which would give a far smaller number; others read the numbers as symbolic or as later idealization. See the note on 1:46 for these views.

a: Is the LORD's hand too short?
p: A hand that is "short" cannot reach. Isaiah uses the same picture twice.
b: In Hebrew a "short hand" means a lack of power (2 Kings 19:26, "short of hand"). God answers Moses' doubt with a question and a promise: "Now you will see." Isaiah repeats the question for the exiles: "Is my hand too short to ransom you?" (Isaiah 50:2), and "Look, the LORD's hand has not grown too short to save" (Isaiah 59:1). This is one of several moments in Numbers where even Moses doubts, which prepares for his failure at the rock in 20:10–12.

a: they prophesied
p: Not foretelling the future, but probably ecstatic speech or behavior: a visible sign the spirit had come.
b: The verb is hitnabbe', a form that can describe ecstatic, unusual behavior that others could see. Saul does the same when the spirit comes on him among a band of prophets (1 Samuel 10:5–13; 1 Samuel 19:20–24). The point is not what the elders said but that everyone could see they had received the spirit and had authority. The last words, "they did not do it again," make it a one-time sign. The Targum and the Vulgate, followed by the KJV, read the same Hebrew letters as "they did not stop" (see the variant). The New Testament sees a fuller fulfillment at Pentecost (Acts 2:4, 17–18).

a: Eldad
p: Two men on the list stayed in the camp and prophesied anyway. A lost book was later written in their names.
b: The text does not say why Eldad and Medad stayed behind. The Sifre and the Talmud say they hid out of humility, feeling unworthy (Sanhedrin 17a). The Talmud also records what they said: some say they prophesied that Moses would die and Joshua would bring Israel into the land, others that they foretold the quail, or the war of Gog and Magog. An early Christian book, the Shepherd of Hermas (Vision 2.3.4, about AD 100–150), quotes a lost "Book of Eldad and Modat": "The Lord is near to those who turn to him." The book itself does not survive.

a: Moses' assistant from his youth
t: From his youth or one of his chosen?
p: The Hebrew can mean "since his youth" or "one of his chosen young men."
b: The word mibbechurav can come from bechurim, "youth" (so most modern versions), or from bachur, "chosen young man" (so the KJV, "one of his young men," and the Septuagint, "the chosen one"). Either way Joshua is Moses' loyal aide (Exodus 24:13; 33:11). His zeal for Moses' honor is like that of John in Mark 9:38: "we saw a man throwing out demons in your name. We kept trying to hinder him." Moses and Jesus give the same answer.

a: If only all the LORD's people were prophets
p: Moses' wish becomes a promise in Joel, and Peter says it is fulfilled at Pentecost.
b: Moses does not guard his own place. He wishes the spirit on everyone. Joel turns the wish into a promise: "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. They will prophesy, your sons and your daughters" (Joel 2:28). Peter quotes Joel on the day of Pentecost (Acts 2:16–18), and Paul tells a whole church, "I wish all of you spoke in tongues, but even more that you prophesied" (1 Corinthians 14:5). Jewish readers see in Moses' words the humility that 12:3 will praise, and many see a hope for the age to come (Numbers Rabbah 15:25).

a: about two cubits above the face of the ground
p: Migrating quail still fly low over Sinai, exhausted, and are easy to catch. "Two cubits" is about three feet.
b: Every spring and autumn huge flocks of common quail cross the Sinai and the Mediterranean between Africa and Europe. Tired from the long flight, they fly low and land in great numbers, and people along the coast have netted them for thousands of years. A cubit is about 18 inches, so two cubits is about three feet. The Hebrew can mean the birds were piled that deep, as some translations take it, or that they flew about three feet off the ground, easy to grab. Rashi takes the second view. Exodus 16:13 tells of an earlier fall of quail.

a: ten homers
p: A homer was a donkey-load. Ten homers is an enormous amount of meat for one person.
b: The homer (chomer, related to chamor, "donkey") was the largest dry measure, probably about what a donkey can carry, but estimates of its size range widely, from about 2 to 6 bushels. Even the person who gathered the least took ten. They "spread them out" to dry them in the sun; Herodotus (2.77) says the Egyptians salted quail and other small birds and ate them raw. The huge amounts show the greed that the next verse punishes.

a: Kibroth Hattaavah
p: The name means "graves of the craving," from the same root as the craving in 11:4.
b: Qivrot hatta'avah means "the graves of the craving." The chapter begins and ends with this root (11:4, 34). Deuteronomy 9:22 names it with Taberah and Massah as places where Israel made the LORD angry. Psalm 78:30–31 says God struck down "the strongest of them" while the food was still in their mouths. The lesson is not that eating meat is wrong (meat is promised in 11:18) but that greed turned a gift into a grave.

a: Miriam and Aaron spoke
p: The verb is feminine and singular: Miriam leads, Aaron joins. That is why she alone is struck.
b: The Hebrew verb vatedabber, "and she spoke," is feminine singular, though two people are its subject. Miriam is named first. The grammar fits the story: she starts the complaint, and only she is struck with the disease (12:10). Aaron, the high priest, confesses and pleads (12:11). Interpreters have asked whether the punishment is fair to Miriam. Some see a double standard, since Aaron also spoke. Others answer that Aaron, as high priest, could not become unclean without leaving the sanctuary, or that the leader of a revolt bears the heavier share. The text itself does not explain.

a: the Cushite woman he had married
p: Was she Zipporah or a second wife from Cush (Nubia)? Jewish, Christian and modern readers have answered differently.
b: Cush is usually the land south of Egypt (Nubia; the Septuagint has "the Ethiopian woman"). Readers divide. (1) She is Zipporah: Habakkuk 3:7 sets "Cushan" beside Midian. (2) She is a second, African wife; Josephus tells of Moses marrying an Ethiopian princess (Antiquities 2.252–253). (3) The rabbis read "Cushite" as praise of her beauty (Sifre; Rashi). (4) Many critical scholars think this verse preserves a separate tradition about Moses' wife, not the Zipporah story. African American interpreters such as Cain Hope Felder and Randall Bailey read the story as God taking the side of a Black woman's marriage against prejudice. Others object that the text never mentions skin, that ancient Israel had no modern idea of race, and that the stated complaint is Moses' authority (12:2). Cushites appear elsewhere without stigma: Ebed-melech the Cushite rescues Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:7–13), and Amos 9:7 sets Cushites beside Israel. Jeremiah 13:23 shows that Cushite skin was noticed.

a: only through Moses
p: Miriam and Aaron had real standing: Miriam is called a prophet, and Micah names all three as Israel's leaders.
b: The complaint is not empty. Exodus 15:20 calls Miriam "the prophet," and Aaron spoke for God to Pharaoh (Exodus 7:1). Micah 6:4 has God say, "I sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam ahead of you." Their question is about authority: is Moses' word above theirs? The marriage in 12:1 seems to be the excuse; the real issue is Moses' unique role. God's answer in 12:6–8 does not deny that Miriam and Aaron hear from God, but sets Moses apart.

a: the man Moses was very humble
t: The humblest man, writing about himself?
p: If Moses wrote this verse, he praised his own humility. This verse is a classic test case for who wrote the Torah.
b: Traditional Jews and Christians hold that Moses wrote the Torah (Bava Batra 14b–15a, which gives the last eight verses of Deuteronomy to Joshua). Some say Moses wrote this line at God's command, as plain fact, not boasting. Others suggest a later inspired editor, perhaps Joshua or Ezra, added it as a comment. Critical scholars see it as one of many signs that someone else, much later, wrote about Moses. The word anav means lowly, humble before God, not weak; the KJV's "meek" is close. Some suggest it means "burdened" or "afflicted," fitting 11:10–15. The written text spells it with an extra letter ('nyw), read as 'anaw, with no change in sense.

a: I make myself known to him in a vision
p: Visions and dreams are real revelation, but less direct than God's speech with Moses.
b: God's answer is set as poetry, and the Plain English shows its lines. Ordinary prophets receive visions (mar'ah) and dreams (chalom). Genesis is full of such dreams (Genesis 28:12; 37:5–9; 41:1). Moses receives something else: speech "mouth to mouth." The first line of the Hebrew is awkward ("If your prophet is the LORD..."). Many scholars repoint it to read "a prophet of the LORD among you," and the Septuagint has "a prophet of yours for the Lord." The point is clear: there are degrees of revelation, and Moses stands at the top.

a: In all my house he is faithful
p: Hebrews quotes this line to compare Moses with Jesus: a servant in the house and a son over it.
b: The word ne'eman means trusted or faithful, like a steward who runs the whole household (compare Joseph in Genesis 39:4–6). Hebrews 3:2–6 quotes the Greek of this verse: "Moses was faithful in all his house, as a servant," but Christ is faithful "as a Son, over his house." Hebrews honors Moses even while it ranks Jesus above him. In Jewish thought this verse grounds the belief that Moses' prophecy is unique; Maimonides made it the seventh of his Thirteen Principles of faith.

a: Mouth to mouth
t: Mouth to mouth, face to face
p: Exodus says "face to face"; here it is "mouth to mouth." Both mean direct speech without a go-between.
b: Exodus 33:11 says the LORD spoke to Moses "face to face, as anyone talks with a close companion," and Deuteronomy 34:10 calls him the prophet "whom the LORD knew face to face." Yet in Exodus 33:20 God also tells Moses, "You cannot see my face." The phrases describe closeness, not a full sight of God. "Mouth to mouth" stresses clear speech, as the next words say: "openly and not in riddles."

a: not in riddles
p: Paul may be echoing the Greek of this verse when he says we now see "in a riddle."
b: The Hebrew chidot are riddles or puzzling sayings (Judges 14:12; Proverbs 1:6). The Septuagint has "not through riddles" (ou di' ainigmatōn). Paul says that now "we see in a mirror, in a riddle (en ainigmati), but then face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Many scholars think Paul has this verse in mind: what Moses had, clear and direct knowledge, is what all believers will have at the end.

a: he looks at the form of the LORD
p: Moses sees God's "form" (temunah). Deuteronomy says the people saw no form at Sinai.
b: The word temunah means a shape or likeness. It is the word used in the command against making images (Exodus 20:4; Deuteronomy 4:12, 15–16: "you saw no form"). Moses alone sees something of God's form, perhaps what Exodus 33:23 calls God's "back." The Septuagint softened the phrase to "he saw the glory of the LORD," and the Targums make it "the likeness of the Glory." Both show the reverence of later readers who did not want God to seem to have a body.

a: struck with a skin disease, like snow
p: The disease is tsara'at, a flaky skin condition, not Hansen's disease. "Like snow" probably means flaking, not white.
b: The Hebrew tsara'at, often translated "leprosy," names a set of scaly skin conditions described in Leviticus 13. It is not the disease now called leprosy. "Like snow" is the same phrase used of Moses' hand in Exodus 4:6 and of Gehazi in 2 Kings 5:27; it likely describes flaking, like snowflakes, more than whiteness. Many readers see an irony after 12:1: Miriam objected to a Cushite woman, and her own skin becomes "like snow." If the phrase means flaking rather than whiteness, the irony is weaker. The rabbis saw the disease as punishment for evil speech (lashon hara), and Deuteronomy 24:9 tells Israel to "remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam."

a: like one who comes out of his mother's womb with half his flesh eaten away
p: Jewish tradition says the original read "our mother" and "our flesh." A sister's disease shames the whole family.
b: Aaron compares Miriam to a stillborn child whose skin has begun to decay. The rabbis list this verse among the "corrections of the scribes" (see 11:15): the original is said to have read "who comes out of our mother's womb" and "half of our flesh," since Miriam, Aaron and Moses had the same mother. The scribes are said to have changed it to the third person to avoid a shameful phrase. No manuscript has this reading. Either way, Aaron's point is that Miriam is family: her disease is like a death in the family.

a: God, please, heal her, please!
p: In Hebrew, Moses' prayer is just five short words. The Talmud says a prayer need not be long.
b: The Hebrew is El na, refa na lah, five short words. The Talmud (Berakhot 34a) uses it to teach that prayer can be very short: when a student complained that a prayer leader was too brief, Rabbi Eliezer answered that Moses prayed for his sister in just these words. The Sifre adds that Moses did not pray long so that people would not say he was busy praying for his sister while Israel waited. The words are still used in Jewish prayers for the sick.
orig: אֵל נָא רְפָא נָא לָהּ (El na refa na lah)

a: If her father had only spit in her face
p: Spitting in someone's face was a public shaming. God argues from the smaller case to the greater.
b: Spitting in the face appears elsewhere as a public disgrace: in the ceremony for a man who refuses to marry his brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:9), and in Job 30:10 and Isaiah 50:6. The argument runs from the lighter to the heavier case (the rabbis' qal vachomer): if a father's insult would shame her for seven days, how much more an insult from God. Genesis Rabbah 92:7 counts this verse among the ten examples of such reasoning in the Bible. Seven days matches the time of isolation in Leviticus 13:4–5.

a: the people did not set out until Miriam was brought back in
p: The Mishnah sees measure for measure: Miriam once waited for baby Moses, so Israel waited for her.
b: The whole camp waits a week for one woman to be healed and brought back. The Mishnah (Sotah 1:9) sees a fitting reward: Miriam waited by the river for an hour to see what would happen to baby Moses (Exodus 2:4), so all Israel waited seven days for her. The text honors Miriam even in her punishment. She is restored, and she is mentioned again only at her death (20:1).

a: the Wilderness of Paran
p: Paran is the large desert of the east-central Sinai, north of the traditional Mount Sinai and south of Canaan.
b: Paran is a broad wilderness between Sinai and the Negev, probably the desert plateau of east-central Sinai (today's Badiyat et-Tih). Ishmael lived there (Genesis 21:21), and the cloud stopped there after Israel left Sinai (10:12). Kadesh, the main camp for the next stories, lies at its northern edge, where it meets the Wilderness of Zin (13:26; 20:1). The Samaritan Pentateuch adds a speech of Moses from Deuteronomy at this point (see the variant).

a: Send men
p: Here God commands it. In Deuteronomy the people ask for it. The rabbis read "send for yourself" as "if you want to."
b: Numbers says the LORD told Moses to send the scouts. Deuteronomy 1:22–23 says the people came to Moses and asked to send men ahead, and Moses agreed. Rashi, following the Talmud (Sotah 34b), joins the two: the Hebrew shelach lekha, "send for yourself," means "send if you choose; I do not command it." God allowed what the people wanted. Source critics see two versions of the story. The Samaritan Pentateuch inserts the Deuteronomy account just before this verse (see the variant at 12:16).

a: to scout out
p: The verb tur means to explore or look over. It returns in 15:39 for the eyes that go scouting after sin.
b: Most English versions call these men "spies," but the main verb here, tur, means to explore or tour a land. (Joshua's men in Joshua 2:1 are true spies, meraggelim.) This verb runs through chapters 13–14 (13:2, 16, 17, 21, 25, 32; 14:6–7, 34, 36, 38) and then returns at the end of chapter 15, where the tassels keep Israel from "scouting after" their own hearts and eyes (15:39). The rabbis saw the link: the scouts' eyes led them astray.

a: Caleb son of Jephunneh
p: Caleb leads Judah, but elsewhere he is called a Kenizzite, a clan linked with Edom.
b: Caleb appears here as Judah's leader, but Numbers 32:12 and Joshua 14:6, 14 call him "the Kenizzite." Kenaz is an Edomite name in Genesis 36:11, 15, 42. Many scholars think Caleb's clan was of outside origin and was taken into Judah. His name may mean "dog," or "whole-hearted" (kol lev), as some later Jewish readers liked to say. He will be one of only two men of his generation to enter the land (14:24, 30).

a: Moses called Hoshea son of Nun "Joshua."
p: Hoshea means "he saves." Joshua means "the LORD saves." In Greek it is Iesous, the same name as Jesus.
b: Hoshea means "he saves" or "salvation." Moses adds the divine name, making Yehoshua, "the LORD saves." The Greek form is Iēsous, which is how the New Testament spells both Joshua (Acts 7:45; Hebrews 4:8) and Jesus. The Talmud says Moses prayed over him, "May God (Yah) save you from the scouts' plan" (Sotah 34b). Justin Martyr saw the renaming as a sign pointing to Jesus (Dialogue with Trypho 113). Exodus 17:9 already calls him Joshua; the text may use his later name there.

a: the Negev
p: Negev is a region, the dry south of Canaan. The KJV turned it into a direction: "southward."
b: Negev literally means "dry land" and became the name of the arid region south of the hill country of Judah, around Beersheba and Arad. Because it lay to the south, the word also came to mean "south," and the KJV translates "go up this way southward." Modern translations keep it as a place name. The scouts were to go up from the desert through the Negev into the hill country around Hebron.

a: from the Wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, near Lebo Hamath
p: This verse sends them to the far north; the next verses mention only Hebron. Readers explain the gap differently.
b: Lebo Hamath, "the entrance of Hamath," is probably Lebweh in the Beqaa Valley of Lebanon, the ideal northern border of the promised land (34:8). That is more than 250 miles from Kadesh, a long trip in forty days. Verses 22–24 speak only of Hebron and the Valley of Eshcol in the south. Source critics see two stories woven together: a Priestly version in which they explore the whole land, and an older one in which they go only as far as Hebron. Traditional readers take verse 21 as a summary of the whole trip and verses 22–24 as one notable part of it.

a: the descendants of Anak
p: The Anakim were remembered as a race of tall warriors around Hebron. Caleb drives them out later.
b: Anak ("necklace" or "long-necked") is the ancestor of the Anakim, remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 21; 9:2). Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai are named again when Caleb drives them out of Hebron (Joshua 15:14; Judges 1:10). Some scholars connect the name with "Iy-'anaq," a place listed in the Egyptian Execration Texts of about 1800 BC, though this link is uncertain. Later Jewish tradition, and the scouts themselves in 13:33, linked the Anakim with the Nephilim of Genesis 6:4.

a: Hebron had been built seven years before Zoan in Egypt
p: Zoan is Tanis in the Nile Delta. Why compare Hebron to an Egyptian city? Scholars are not sure.
b: Zoan is the Hebrew name for Tanis, in the eastern Nile Delta (Psalm 78:12, 43). Tanis became a royal city in the 21st Dynasty, about 1070 BC, though the region was settled much earlier. Hebron was already a walled city in the Middle Bronze Age, about 1800–1550 BC, as excavations at Tel Rumeida show. The comparison may reflect a now-lost tradition about the founding dates of the two cities, perhaps linked to the earlier city of Avaris near Tanis. The rabbis read it as praise of the land (Sotah 34b; Rashi). The same page notes that "he came to Hebron" is singular, and says Caleb went alone to pray at the patriarchs' graves.

a: a single cluster of grapes
p: Two men carrying a huge cluster became a symbol of the land's richness, and for Christians, of the cross.
b: The Talmud says eight men carried the grapes (Sotah 34a), but the text says only that it took a pole and two bearers. The image of the two scouts with the giant cluster is used today as the logo of Israel's Ministry of Tourism. Early and medieval Christians read it as a picture of Christ, the "cluster" hanging on the wood, with the man in front (who cannot see it) as the synagogue and the man behind (who can) as the church. Eshcol means "cluster"; there is still a rich vineyard region north of Hebron.

a: at Kadesh
p: Kadesh was Israel's base for much of the wilderness time, usually placed at springs in northeastern Sinai.
b: Kadesh, also called Kadesh-barnea (32:8; Deuteronomy 1:2, 19), is usually placed at Ein el-Qudeirat, the richest spring in northeastern Sinai, near Ein Qadeis, which keeps the ancient name. Excavations at Tell el-Qudeirat by Rudolph Cohen and others found a series of Israelite fortresses from about the 10th to the 6th centuries BC, but nothing from the Late Bronze Age, when most date the exodus. Those who take the story as history answer that a camp of tents would leave little trace. Deuteronomy 1:46 says Israel stayed at Kadesh "many days."

a: milk and honey
p: Milk from goats and sheep; honey from bees and dates. Archaeologists have found ancient beehives in Israel.
b: "A land flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8) describes a land good for herds and orchards. "Milk" is mostly from goats and sheep. "Honey" (devash) can be bee honey or sweet syrup from dates and figs, which the rabbis often took it to mean. Bees were certainly kept: at Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley, archaeologists found an apiary of about 10th–9th century BC with dozens of clay hives. The scouts confirm God's promise, then undercut it with "But" in the next verse.

a: Amalek lives in the land of the Negev
p: The scouts map the peoples: raiders in the south, hill peoples in the middle, Canaanites in the lowlands.
b: Amalek, the old enemy (Exodus 17:8–16), roams the southern desert. The Hittites here are not the empire of Anatolia but a local group, as in Genesis 23. The Jebusites held Jerusalem until David (2 Samuel 5:6–9). "Amorite" is used loosely for hill peoples, and "Canaanite" for those in the lowlands. The list sets up 14:25, 43–45, where Amalekites and Canaanites defeat Israel.

a: Caleb hushed the people
p: The Hebrew verb is the sound of hushing a crowd, like "shh."
b: The verb vayyahas comes from has, "Hush!" (Judges 3:19; Amos 6:10), a sound word like English "shh." Caleb quiets the crowd before answering the report. The Talmud (Sotah 35a) imagines him getting their attention by pretending to join the complaint: "Is this all the son of Amram has done to us?" Then, when they fell silent to listen, he praised what Moses had done. Joshua is not mentioned here and joins Caleb only in 14:6.

a: a land that eats up the people who live there
t: A land that eats its people
p: Did the scouts mean the land was unhealthy, war-torn, or simply that they were afraid? Readers differ.
b: The phrase can mean the land is so fought over that its people die in wars, or that it is barren and unhealthy, which contradicts the giant grapes. Ezekiel uses the same words of a land that "eats people" and robs its nation of children (Ezekiel 36:13–14), and God promises to end that reproach. The Talmud (Sotah 35a) says the scouts saw funerals everywhere because God had caused the leading Canaanites to die so the scouts would pass unnoticed, and they twisted a kindness into a slander. The text calls their report a dibbah, a slander or whispered evil report.
orig: דִּבַּת הָאָרֶץ (dibbat ha'arets), "the evil report of the land"

a: There we saw the Nephilim
p: The Nephilim of Genesis 6 were wiped out by the flood. The scouts' claim may be fear speaking.
b: Genesis 6:4 says "the Nephilim were on the earth" in the days before the flood, "the heroes of ancient times, men with a name." The word may mean "fallen ones"; the Septuagint has "giants." If the flood destroyed all humankind but Noah's family, how could Nephilim be in Canaan? Some rabbis said a giant, Og, survived the flood (Niddah 61a). Many modern commentators think the scouts are exaggerating: the people were tall, and fear turned them into monsters from old stories. The Plain English keeps "descendants of Anak, who come from the Nephilim," which the Greek lacks (see the variant).

a: like grasshoppers
p: The scouts saw themselves as tiny. Isaiah later uses the same image for all people before God.
b: Grasshoppers are small, weak and easily crushed. The scouts say first how they saw themselves, then how they think the giants saw them. In the Talmud, Rav Mesharsheya says the scouts were liars: they could know how they looked to themselves, but how could they know how they looked to the giants (Sotah 35a)? A midrash has God himself object: "Who told you how I made you look in their eyes?" (Tanhuma, Shelach 7). Isaiah 40:22 turns the image upside down: before God who sits above the earth, all its people are like grasshoppers, so no human giant need be feared.

a: the people wept that night
t: The night of the Ninth of Av
p: The Talmud dates this night of weeping to the Ninth of Av, later the day of mourning for the temple.
b: Jewish tradition counts the days: the scouts left in late spring (13:20, "the season of the first ripe grapes"), and forty days later they returned. The Talmud (Taanit 29a) places this night on the Ninth of Av and has God say: "You wept for nothing; I will give you a reason to weep for all generations." The Mishnah lists five disasters on that date, the first being the decree that this generation would not enter the land (Taanit 4:6). Both temples were later destroyed on or near that day, and Jews still fast and mourn on Tisha B'Av.

a: Let's appoint a leader and go back to Egypt
p: Nehemiah remembers this as the people choosing a leader "to return to their slavery."
b: Going back to Egypt would undo the exodus. Nehemiah 9:17 recalls the moment: "They appointed a leader to go back to their slavery." Stephen says the same in Acts 7:39: they "turned their hearts back toward Egypt." Deuteronomy 17:16 later forbids a king to lead the people back to Egypt. For the rabbis, the wish to return was the low point of the wilderness.

a: they are our bread
p: To call enemies "our bread" means they will be easy to swallow up. It answers the scouts' "a land that eats."
b: Joshua and Caleb turn the scouts' words around. The scouts said the land "eats up" its people (13:32); Joshua and Caleb say the people of the land will be "our bread," food we will eat. Psalm 14:4 and Micah 3:3 use eating as a picture of conquering or exploiting. The Septuagint has "they are food for us."
orig: לַחְמֵנוּ הֵם (lachmenu hem), "they are our bread"

a: Their shade has turned away from them
p: "Shade" is protection, as shade protects from the desert sun. The Canaanites' gods, or their luck, have left them.
b: In a hot land, shade means shelter and safety: "The LORD is your shade at your right side" (Psalm 121:5; compare Isaiah 30:2). Joshua and Caleb mean that whatever protected the Canaanites has left them. Rashi says their protectors were their righteous men, who had died; Targum Onqelos has "their strength has departed." Others think of the Canaanites' gods, as when Egypt's gods were judged (33:4).
orig: סָר צִלָּם (sar tsillam), "their shade has turned aside"

a: the glory of the LORD appeared at the tent of meeting
p: In Numbers, God's glory appears when the people revolt, to judge and to stop the revolt.
b: At Sinai the glory filled the tabernacle as a sign of God's presence (Exodus 40:34–35). In Numbers it appears again and again at moments of revolt: here, at Korah's rebellion (16:19, 42), and at the waters of Meribah (20:6). Each time it comes just as the people are about to do violence or as God is about to judge. The glory is both protection for God's servants and a threat to rebels.

a: I will make you into a nation greater and mightier than they are
p: God makes Moses the same offer he made after the golden calf. Moses refuses again.
b: After the golden calf God said to Moses, "I will make you into a great nation" (Exodus 32:10). Here the offer returns, even larger: "greater and mightier than they are." Both times Moses refuses and pleads for the people, using the same arguments: what will Egypt say (Exodus 32:12), and God's own character (Exodus 34:6–7). Jewish and Christian readers see in this a mark of the true leader, who will not build himself up on his people's ruin.

a: seen eye to eye
p: The Hebrew is "eye in eye": God was seen up close, openly.
b: The phrase ayin be'ayin means seeing directly, at close range. Isaiah uses it for the watchmen who will see the LORD's return to Zion "eye to eye" (Isaiah 52:8). In everyday English, "see eye to eye" means to agree, which is not the sense here; the point is that God's presence among Israel was plain to see, in the cloud by day and fire by night (Exodus 13:21–22). Moses argues that the nations know this, so God's reputation is bound up with Israel.

a: let the Lord's power be great
p: In Hebrew Bibles, one letter in the word "be great" is written larger than the rest.
b: In the Masoretic Text the first letter, yod, of yigdal, "may it be great," is written larger than normal. The Masoretes marked a few such letters in the Bible (for example the first letter of Genesis and the last letter of the first word of the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4). Their purpose is debated; most were probably meant to draw attention to a verse. Here Moses appeals to God's power, not to show force, but to forgive. Here the title is Adonai, "the Lord," not the divine name.

a: The LORD is slow to anger and great in loyal love
p: Moses quotes Exodus 34:6–7, but he leaves some words out. What he leaves out has been much discussed.
b: God announced his character to Moses in Exodus 34:6–7: "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, great in loyal love and faithfulness, keeping loyal love to thousands, forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin." Here Moses quotes it in short form. He leaves out "compassionate and gracious," "faithfulness" and "keeping loyal love to thousands," and he keeps the warning about punishment to the fourth generation. That warning comes true in this very chapter: the parents die in the wilderness, and the children wander forty years (14:33). The same creed echoes in Joel 2:13, Jonah 4:2, Nahum 1:3 and Psalm 103:8.
r: Exodus 34:6–7; Exodus 20:5–6; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2; Nahum 1:3; Psalm 86:15; Psalm 103:8; Nehemiah 9:17

a: I have forgiven, as you asked
p: Jews recite these words on the eve of the Day of Atonement, right after Kol Nidre.
b: On the evening that begins Yom Kippur, after the Kol Nidre prayer, the congregation recites 15:26 ("the whole community of Israelites will be forgiven"), and the leader recites 14:19, Moses' plea. Then all respond with 14:20: Salachti kidvarekha, "I have forgiven, as you asked." The words carry hope that God will forgive again. Yet the verse goes on: forgiveness here means Israel is not wiped out, but the guilty generation still dies in the wilderness. Forgiveness and consequences stand side by side.

a: the LORD's glory will fill all the earth
t: The whole earth full of glory
p: In the middle of judgment, God swears that his glory will fill the earth. The prophets and Psalms repeat it.
b: God takes an oath on his own life and on the hope that his glory will fill all the earth. The line points beyond this failed generation to God's purpose for the world. Isaiah's seraphim sing that "Everything that fills the earth is his glory" (Isaiah 6:3), Habakkuk 2:14 says the earth will be filled "with knowing the glory of the LORD, as waters cover the sea," and Psalm 72:19 prays for it. The rebellion of one generation will not defeat that plan.

a: these ten times
p: "Ten times" may mean "over and over." The rabbis counted ten actual tests.
b: "Ten times" can be a round number for "many times," as when Jacob says Laban "changed my wages ten times" (Genesis 31:7). The rabbis counted ten real tests in the wilderness: two at the sea, two over water, two over manna, two over quail, the golden calf and the scouts (Mishnah Avot 5:4; Arakhin 15a–b). Some modern readers think the number is symbolic, matching the ten plagues: God tested Egypt ten times, and Israel tested God ten times.

a: None of those who spurned me will see it
p: Psalm 95 and the letter to the Hebrews make this verdict a warning to every later generation.
b: Psalm 95:8–11 calls worshipers not to harden their hearts "as at Meribah, as on the day of Massah," and ends with God's oath: "they will not enter my rest." Hebrews 3:7–4:11 quotes the psalm and applies it to Christians: the wilderness generation "could not enter because of unbelief" (Hebrews 3:19), so "let us be eager to enter that rest" (Hebrews 4:11). Paul too uses the bodies in the desert as a warning (1 Corinthians 10:5), and Jude 5 says the Lord "destroyed those who did not believe."
r: Psalm 95:7–11; Hebrews 3:7–19; Hebrews 4:1–11; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11; Jude 5; Psalm 106:24–26

a: he followed me fully
p: The Hebrew idiom is "he filled after me": complete, undivided loyalty. It becomes Caleb's motto.
b: The phrase vayemalle acharai, literally "he filled after me," means following God completely, with nothing held back. It is used of Caleb again and again (32:12; Deuteronomy 1:36; Joshua 14:8, 9, 14), and once of Joshua with him (32:12). The "different spirit" is not explained. Rashi, drawing on the Tanhuma, says Caleb had two spirits, one in his mouth and one in his heart: he seemed to agree with the scouts but did not. Many Christian readers see in Caleb a model of faith that holds when others fail.
orig: וַיְמַלֵּא אַחֲרָי (vayemalle acharai), "he filled after me"

a: the road to the Sea of Reeds
p: Here the "Sea of Reeds" is probably the Gulf of Aqaba, the eastern arm of the Red Sea, not the sea Israel crossed.
b: Yam Suf, the "Sea of Reeds," is the sea crossed in Exodus 14–15. But the Bible also uses the name for the Gulf of Aqaba: King Solomon's port of Ezion-geber was "on the shore of the Sea of Reeds in the land of Edom" (1 Kings 9:26). "The road to the Sea of Reeds" here and in 21:4 is probably a route southeast from Kadesh toward the Gulf of Aqaba. Israel is sent away from Canaan, back into the desert. The Septuagint and KJV have "the Red Sea."

a: from twenty years old and up
p: The sentence falls on those counted in the census. The rabbis said the Levites and the women were spared.
b: The verdict applies to those counted in the census of chapter 1, the men twenty and older (1:3). Rashi notes that the tribe of Levi was not counted in that census (1:47–49), and the Talmud concludes that the Levites were not included in the decree (Bava Batra 121b), which would explain how Eleazar the priest lived to enter the land (Joshua 14:1). A midrash says the women were spared too, because they loved the land and did not join the revolt; the daughters of Zelophehad ask for land in 27:1–11 (Numbers Rabbah 21:10). The census of chapter 26 confirms that none of the counted men but Caleb and Joshua remained (26:64–65).

a: They will suffer for your prostitution
p: The word is zenut, "prostitution": disloyalty pictured as adultery. The children bear its results.
b: The Hebrew zenutekhem, "your acts of prostitution," pictures Israel's rejection of God as adultery, an image the prophets later develop (Hosea 1–3; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The children "bear" it (Hebrew nasa): they suffer the results, wandering forty years though they did not join the revolt. This fits Exodus 34:7 (quoted in 14:18). Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20 say each person dies for his own sin; most readers reconcile the texts by saying the children share the consequences but not the guilt, and in the end they enter the land (14:31).

a: a day for a year, a day for a year
p: Forty days of scouting become forty years of wandering. Some later interpreters made this a key to prophetic time.
b: The punishment matches the sin: one year for each day of scouting. Ezekiel 4:5–6 uses the same rule when he lies on his side, "a day for each year." Many Protestant interpreters from the 1500s on, and especially the Millerites and Seventh-day Adventists in the 1800s, used these two texts to read the "days" of Daniel and Revelation as years (the "day-year principle"). Most scholars, Jewish and Christian, think the two passages apply the rule only to their own cases and do not set a general key for prophecy.

a: learn what it means when I oppose you
p: The rare Hebrew word means God's turning against them. It appears again only once, in Job.
b: The noun tenu'ah appears only here and in Job 33:10, where Job is said to complain that God finds "pretexts" against him. It comes from a verb meaning to hinder or frustrate (32:7, 9; 30:5). The KJV has "my breach of promise," the Septuagint "the wrath of my anger." The sense is that Israel will learn by experience what it means for God to oppose them, as he has so far fought for them.

a: they dared to go up
p: The rare verb means to swell or presume. Habakkuk uses the same root for the proud who are not upright.
b: The verb vayya'pilu is found only here. It is linked with 'ophel, a mound or swelling, and with Habakkuk 2:4: "Look, the one who is swollen with pride: the soul inside him is not upright. But the righteous will live by his faithfulness." Here "swollen" is 'uppelah. Paul quotes the second half of that line (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11), and Hebrews quotes it with this context (Hebrews 10:38). Deuteronomy 1:43 uses another word: "you acted presumptuously." Faith obeys God's word when he says go (14:9) and when he says do not go (14:42).

a: the ark of the LORD's covenant and Moses did not move
p: The ark led Israel in battle. Here it stays behind, a sign that God is not going with them.
b: When the ark set out, Moses would say, "Rise up, LORD! Let your enemies scatter" (10:35). Going to war without the ark and without Moses means going without God. A later disaster shows the opposite mistake: Israel took the ark into battle like a lucky charm and lost it to the Philistines (1 Samuel 4:3–11). In both stories, what matters is obeying God, not carrying the right objects.

a: as far as Hormah
p: Hormah means "devoted to destruction." Its name is explained again in 21:3 and Judges 1:17.
b: Hormah, from cherem, "devoted to destruction," was a town in the eastern Negev. Its site is uncertain; Tel Masos and Tel Halif have been proposed. The town gets its name in 21:3 after Israel destroys it, and again in Judges 1:17, after Judah and Simeon destroy Zephath. Here the name is used ahead of time. Deuteronomy 1:44 adds that the enemy "chased you the way bees do." The Samaritan Pentateuch adds lines from Deuteronomy after 14:40 and after 14:45 (see the variants).

a: You are going to come into the land where you will live
t: Laws for a land they will reach
p: Right after the verdict of chapter 14, God gives laws for life in the land. Readers see a promise in it.
b: Chapter 15 can seem out of place between the scouts and Korah. Ramban and many later readers see its placement as comfort: the parents will die, but God's laws for life in the land assume the children will get there. Source critics see a Priestly collection added to the story, and note that 15:1–16 updates the offerings of Leviticus with fixed amounts of grain, oil and wine. The rabbis also read 15:22–31 as a lesson after rebellion: sins by mistake can be forgiven, but defiant sin cuts a person off.

a: a soothing smell for the LORD
p: The phrase means an offering God accepts with pleasure. It first appears after the flood.
b: Reach nichoach, "a soothing smell," first appears when Noah offers sacrifices after the flood and "the LORD smelled the soothing smell" (Genesis 8:21), with a play on Noah's name (nuach, "rest"). It describes an offering that pleases God and calms his anger. The image is bold, and the Targums soften it to "received with favor." Paul applies it to Christ, who "handed himself over for us, an offering and sacrifice to God with a sweet smell" (Ephesians 5:2), and to the gifts of believers (Philippians 4:18).

a: the drink offering
p: The drink offering was wine poured out at the altar. Paul uses it as a picture of giving his life.
b: Here every burnt offering and peace offering comes with a grain offering and a drink offering (nesekh), and the amounts grow with the size of the animal: a quarter of a hin of wine for a lamb, a third for a ram, a half for a bull. The wine was probably poured out at the base of the altar (Sirach 50:15). Paul writes, "even if my life is poured out over the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad" (Philippians 2:17), and near his death, "I am already being poured out" (2 Timothy 4:6).

a: one rule for you and for the foreigner
p: The ger was a foreigner living in Israel. The rabbis read the word as a convert.
b: A ger is a foreigner who has come to live among Israel without land or family there, a resident alien. This passage says the same rules for offerings apply to him as to the native Israelite (compare Exodus 12:49; Leviticus 24:22). The rabbis read ger in such laws as a full convert (ger tsedeq), so that the verse means converts are equal to born Jews; the Septuagint already translates it prosēlytos, "one who has come over." Modern readers often stress the original social sense: Israel's law protects and includes outsiders.

a: From the first of your dough, set aside a loaf as a gift
p: This is the origin of challah. Paul uses the image: if the first piece of dough is holy, so is the whole batch.
b: The first part of each batch of dough was to be given to God, that is, to the priests. A whole tractate of the Mishnah, Challah, works out the details (for example, a minimum amount of dough). The Mishnah lists separating challah as one of three commandments especially given to women (Shabbat 2:6), and observant Jews still break off a small piece and burn it. The braided Sabbath loaf took its name from this gift. Paul writes, "If the firstfruit is holy, the whole lump of dough is holy too" (Romans 11:16), meaning Israel's founders make the people holy.

a: Now if you go astray
p: Leviticus 4 covers the community's mistakes with different offerings. Rabbis and scholars explain why.
b: Leviticus 4:13–21 requires a bull as a sin offering when the whole community sins by mistake. Here the community brings a bull as a burnt offering and a goat as a sin offering. The rabbis solved the difference by subject: Leviticus 4 covers ordinary commandments, while this passage, with its wording "all these commands," covers mistaken idolatry, which breaks the whole law (Horayot 8a; Sifre; Rashi). Many critical scholars think the two passages come from different stages of priestly law, this one later.

a: by mistake
p: The Hebrew shegagah means a slip, a wrong done without meaning to. It is not the same as defiant sin.
b: Shegagah covers wrongs done in ignorance or by accident: a person did not know the rule, or did not know he was breaking it. Such sins still need atonement, because they still harm one's relation to God and pollute the sanctuary, but offerings can deal with them. The contrast is "with a high hand" (15:30). The same idea of unintended killing lies behind the cities of refuge (35:11). Jesus' prayer from the cross, "they do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34), and Peter's "you acted in ignorance" (Acts 3:17) draw on this category.

a: with a high hand
p: A raised fist: deliberate, open defiance. Israel left Egypt with a high hand; now it describes defying God.
b: The phrase beyad ramah pictures a hand raised in defiance. Exodus 14:8 used it for Israel leaving Egypt boldly, "with a hand raised high." Here it means sinning knowingly and openly, which "insults" (megaddef, "reviles") the LORD. No offering is given for such sin. Psalm 19:13 prays, "Hold your servant back from arrogant sins too." Hebrews 10:26 says that "if we keep sinning willfully after we have received knowledge of the truth, there is no sacrifice left for sins." The rabbis taught that repentance and the Day of Atonement can still bring forgiveness even for deliberate sins (Mishnah Yoma 8:8–9).

a: That person will be cut off from among his people
p: The penalty of karet is debated: death by God's hand, dying young, having no descendants, or loss of the world to come.
b: The phrase "cut off" (karet) is used for many serious sins in the Torah. It is usually not a human court's sentence. The rabbis took it as a punishment from heaven: early death, or dying without children (Mishnah Keritot 1:1 lists thirty-six such sins; Moed Katan 28a). Maimonides and others held that the soul itself is cut off from the world to come. Some modern scholars think it once meant being banished from the community. Milgrom argues it means God ends a person's family line. The text itself does not define it.

a: a man gathering wood on the Sabbath day
p: The story follows the law on defiant sin as an example. Rabbis and Christians have struggled with its harshness.
b: Exodus 31:14–15 and 35:2–3 already set death for Sabbath work and forbid lighting fires. So why the question (15:34)? Rashi says they knew he must die but not how. Rabbi Akiva identified the man as Zelophehad (27:3), whose daughters later inherit land, though others criticized him for naming a sinner the text left unnamed (Shabbat 96b). Some rabbis said he acted to show the people that the Sabbath law still held. Placed after 15:30, the story shows a sin "with a high hand." Christians often contrast it with Jesus, who said "The Sabbath came into being for the sake of human beings" (Mark 2:27).

a: it had not been made clear what should be done to him
p: This is one of four cases in the Torah where Moses must ask God what to do.
b: Four times Moses has no ruling and waits for God: the blasphemer (Leviticus 24:12), the men who were unclean at Passover (9:6–8), this wood gatherer, and the daughters of Zelophehad (27:1–5). The rabbis saw them as models for judges who should not be ashamed to say "I do not know." The wording here matches Leviticus 24:12: "They kept him under guard." In both cases the sentence is stoning outside the camp.

a: tassels
p: Tsitsit are the tassels Jews still wear on the corners of the prayer shawl. Jesus wore them too.
b: The tsitsit were tassels on the four corners of the outer garment (Deuteronomy 22:12). Ancient Near Eastern art shows nobles with fancy tassels and hems as signs of rank; here every Israelite wears one, a sign that the whole people is royal and holy. Jews still wear them on the tallit (prayer shawl) and on a small garment under the clothes. The woman with bleeding touched the "edge" of Jesus' cloak, probably the tassel (Matthew 9:20; 14:36), and Jesus criticized those who "make their tassels long" for show (Matthew 23:5).
r: Deuteronomy 22:12; Matthew 9:20; Matthew 14:36; Matthew 23:5; Mark 6:56; Zechariah 8:23

a: a cord of blue-violet
p: The dye came from a sea snail. Its making was lost for centuries, and some say it has been found again.
b: Tekhelet is the blue-violet dye used in the tabernacle curtains and the high priest's robe (Exodus 26:1; 28:31). It was made from sea snails, very costly, a color of kings. The Talmud says it came from a creature called the chilazon (Menachot 42b–44a), and after about the 7th century AD Jews no longer knew how to make it, so most tassels became all white. In the 20th century researchers, beginning with Rabbi Isaac Herzog's study (1913), identified the snail as the banded dye-murex (Hexaplex trunculus). Some Jews now wear blue threads again; many others do not accept the identification.

a: You will not go scouting after your own heart and your own eyes
p: "Go scouting" is the same verb used for the twelve scouts. The tassels guard against what the scouts did.
b: The verb is tur, the word for the scouts' mission (13:2, 16, 17, 21, 25, 32; 14:34). The scouts went "scouting" and came back with a report that led the people away from God; the tassels are meant to keep Israel's heart and eyes from "scouting" after things that lead astray. "Like a prostitute" uses the root zanah again (14:33). Rashi, drawing on the Tanhuma and the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot 1:5), puts it this way: the heart and the eyes are the body's go-betweens; the eye sees, the heart desires, and the body acts. The Sifre and the Talmud (Berakhot 12b) read "heart" as heresy and "eyes" as lust. Jesus' teaching on the eye and the heart (Matthew 5:28–29) runs along the same lines.
orig: וְלֹא־תָתוּרוּ (velo taturu), "and you will not scout"

a: I am the LORD your God
p: Verses 37–41 are the third paragraph of the Shema, said by observant Jews every morning and evening.
b: The Shema, Judaism's central prayer, has three paragraphs: Deuteronomy 6:4–9, Deuteronomy 11:13–21, and this passage, Numbers 15:37–41. The Mishnah already assumes it is recited daily (Berakhot 1:5–2:2), and the rabbis said it was included because it mentions the exodus. The words "I am the LORD your God" frame the passage at both ends: the tassels and the commands rest on who God is and what he has done.

a: took men
p: The Hebrew says only "Korah took," with no object. What he took has puzzled readers for centuries.
b: The verse opens vayyiqqach Qorach, "Korah took," and never says what. Ibn Ezra and the KJV supply "men," as the Plain English does. Rashi reads it as "he took himself aside," separating from the community; Targum Onqelos has "he divided himself." Many modern scholars suspect a copying slip and suggest "he rose up" (vayyaqom), which fits 16:2. The Septuagint reads "and Korah spoke." However it is solved, the verb pairs with the end of 16:2: Korah took, and they rose up.

a: Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth
p: Levites want the priesthood; Reubenites want political power. Critics see two or three stories woven into one.
b: Korah is a Levite of Kohath's clan, a cousin of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:18–21), and his complaint is about the priesthood (16:8–11). Dathan and Abiram are from Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and their complaint is about Moses' rule and the failed promise of land (16:12–14). Many scholars see an older story of a lay revolt by Dathan and Abiram (the earth swallows them, as Deuteronomy 11:6 remembers without Korah) joined to a Priestly story of Korah and the 250 with fire pans. Traditional readers see one revolt by an alliance of the discontented. On son of Peleth vanishes; the Talmud says his wife talked him out of it (Sanhedrin 109b).

a: men with a name
p: The same words describe the Nephilim in Genesis 6:4. Famous men who rose up against God.
b: "Men with a name" (anshe shem), that is, famous men, is the phrase Genesis 6:4 uses for the Nephilim, "the heroes of ancient times." The builders of Babel also wanted to "make a name" for themselves (Genesis 11:4). The echo may be deliberate: the 250 are leaders with fame, and like the earlier "men with a name," they reach for what is not theirs. They are "chosen for the assembly," probably delegates who were summoned to the council.

a: The whole community is holy
p: Korah quotes something true: God called all Israel holy. The question is what follows from it.
b: God did call all Israel "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:6), and the tassels law has just said "you will be holy to your God" (15:40). Korah draws the conclusion that no one should stand above the rest. The Mishnah names "the dispute of Korah and his band" as the model of a quarrel "not for the sake of heaven" (Avot 5:17). A midrash has Korah mock the tassels law: if a garment is all blue, does it still need a blue thread? (Numbers Rabbah 18:3; Tanhuma). Some modern readers find a real democratic voice in Korah. The story answers that holiness is God's gift, and God chooses who serves at the altar (16:5).
r: Exodus 19:6; 15:40; Leviticus 11:44; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6; Mishnah Avot 5:17

a: the LORD will make known who is his
t: "The Lord knows those who are his"
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this verse in 2 Timothy, about false teachers in the church.
b: The Septuagint renders the first words "God has known those who are his" (egnō ho theos tous ontas autou). 2 Timothy 2:19 quotes almost these words as an inscription on God's firm foundation: "The Lord knows the ones who are his," followed by "Everyone who names the name of the Lord must turn away from wrongdoing," which may echo 16:26 ("Turn away... from the tents of these wicked men"). The letter applies the Korah story to people in the church who were teaching falsely.

a: take fire pans for yourselves
p: The test recalls Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons who died offering incense God had not commanded.
b: A fire pan (machtah; KJV "censer") was a metal pan for carrying coals. Burning incense was the priests' task alone (Exodus 30:7–8). Moses' test has a frightening precedent: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu "each took his fire pan," brought "strange fire" before the LORD, and "Fire came out from before the LORD and ate them up" (Leviticus 10:2). The same fate awaits the 250 (16:35). Later, King Uzziah tried to burn incense and was struck with skin disease (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

a: a land flowing with milk and honey
t: Egypt as the land of milk and honey
p: Dathan and Abiram use God's own words for the promised land to describe Egypt.
b: This is the only time the Bible calls Egypt "a land flowing with milk and honey." The phrase belongs to Canaan (Exodus 3:8; 13:27). Dathan and Abiram turn it upside down: Moses brought them out of paradise to die in the desert, and has not brought them into any promised land (16:14). Their bitter joke shows how far memory had been twisted since 11:5. Their words "make yourself prince over us" echo what an Israelite said to young Moses in Egypt: "Who put you as a chief and a judge over us?" (Exodus 2:14).

a: Will you gouge out the eyes of these men?
p: This may mean "Will you blind us to what you are doing?" or refer to blinding as punishment for rebels.
b: Literally, "Will you bore out the eyes of those men?" Two readings are common. (1) It is an idiom for deceiving: "Do you think you can hoodwink these men?" (2) It refers to the real practice of blinding rebels and captives (Judges 16:21; 1 Samuel 11:2; 2 Kings 25:7), as if to say, "Will you mutilate anyone who disagrees?" "These men" may be a polite way of saying "us." Either way, Dathan and Abiram accuse Moses of tyranny.
orig: הַעֵינֵי הָאֲנָשִׁים הָהֵם תְּנַקֵּר (ha'ene ha'anashim hahem tenaqqer)

a: I have not taken one donkey from them
p: Samuel makes the same defense when he gives up leadership. The Greek reads "desire" instead of "donkey."
b: Moses denies using his office for gain. Samuel says nearly the same thing at the end of his leadership: "Whose ox did I take? Whose donkey did I take?" (1 Samuel 12:3). Paul too reminds churches that he did not seek their money (Acts 20:33; 1 Corinthians 9:12). The Septuagint reads "I have not taken the desire of any of them," reflecting chamud, "desired thing," for chamor, "donkey" (see the variant).

a: God of the spirits of all flesh
t: God of the spirits of all flesh
p: A rare title for God as the giver of life to every creature. Moses and Aaron plead like Abraham at Sodom.
b: This title appears only here and in 27:16. It names God as the source of the life-breath of every creature, who therefore knows each heart. Hebrews 12:9 calls God "the Father of spirits." The plea, "when one man sins, will you be angry with the whole community?" echoes Abraham's question: "Will you really sweep away the righteous along with the wicked?" (Genesis 18:23–25). God answers by separating the guilty from the rest (16:24). Rashi pictures God as a king who knows exactly who sinned.

a: the dwelling of Korah, Dathan and Abiram
p: The word for "dwelling" is mishkan, the same word used for God's tabernacle.
b: Elsewhere in Numbers mishkan nearly always means the LORD's tabernacle. Here, and in 16:27, it is used for the shared "dwelling" of the rebels. Some scholars think the story once spoke of a rival sanctuary set up by Korah. Others think mishkan is simply a word for tent or home, as in Psalm 78:28 and Isaiah 54:2, and that "Korah" was added here when two stories were joined. The Septuagint has "the assembly of Korah." The irony stands either way: the people must step back from a false sanctuary.

a: the LORD may create something new
p: Moses asks for something never seen before. The rabbis said the earth's mouth was made on the first Sabbath eve.
b: The Hebrew is "if the LORD creates a creation" (beri'ah yivra'), using the verb of Genesis 1:1, which in the Bible only ever has God as subject. Moses asks God to prove his mission with an event no one could fake. The Mishnah lists "the mouth of the earth" among ten things God created at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath, made ready for this moment (Avot 5:6). Critical readers note that the earth "opening its mouth" uses the language of ancient poems about the underworld swallowing the living (compare Psalm 106:17; Proverbs 1:12).
r: Genesis 1:1; Exodus 34:10; Isaiah 43:19; Mishnah Avot 5:6; Psalm 106:17; Proverbs 1:12

a: they go down alive to Sheol
p: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead, pictured below the earth. Going there alive is a horror.
b: This is the first time Sheol appears in Numbers. It is the shadowy world of the dead beneath the earth, where Jacob expected to go "still mourning" (Genesis 37:35). The KJV here has "the pit." To go down there alive reverses the normal order of life and death. Psalm 55:15 prays of enemies, "let them go down to Sheol alive," and Proverbs 1:12 puts the image in the mouth of robbers. The story does not describe what happens to the rebels there; the point is that they vanish from the community (16:33).

a: every person who was Korah's
p: This verse sounds as if all Korah's people died, but 26:11 says Korah's sons did not. Their descendants wrote psalms.
b: "Every person who was Korah's" could include his family, but 26:11 says plainly, "the sons of Korah did not die." Rabbis explained that his sons repented at the last moment and were saved on a ledge in Sheol, from which they sang (Sanhedrin 110a; Rashi on 26:11). Their descendants became temple gatekeepers and singers (1 Chronicles 9:19; 2 Chronicles 20:19), and eleven psalms (Psalms 42, 44–49, 84, 85, 87, 88) bear the title "of the sons of Korah." Psalm 46, "God is a shelter and strength for us... So we will have no fear when the earth changes place," reads movingly from that family. The prophet Samuel was also traced to Korah (1 Chronicles 6:22–28).
r: 26:9–11; 1 Chronicles 6:22–28; 1 Chronicles 9:19; Psalm 42; Psalm 46:1–2; Psalm 84; Psalm 88

a: they were gone from among the assembly
p: Jude names Korah with Cain and Balaam as models of those who rebel against God's order.
b: Jude 11 warns of false teachers: "They have walked the road Cain walked. For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error. They have perished in Korah's revolt." The Greek word for revolt, antilogia, means "speaking against," and the verb "perished" (apōlonto) echoes the Septuagint here. For Jude, the story shows what happens to those who reject authority God has set up. Psalm 106:16–18 and Sirach 45:18–19 also remember the scene.

a: hammered into thin sheets as a covering for the altar
p: Exodus already says the altar was overlaid with bronze. Readers explain how it got another covering.
b: Exodus 27:2 and 38:2 say the altar of burnt offering was overlaid with bronze from the start. How can the fire pans become its covering? Many traditional readers say the plates were an extra layer, a visible memorial added over the first. Critical scholars see two traditions: in this one the altar's bronze plating comes from Korah's fire pans, and the Exodus account was written with the finished altar in view. Once offered to the LORD, even rebels' fire pans were holy and could not be thrown away (16:37).

a: No outsider, no one who is not of Aaron's offspring
p: Zar, "outsider," means anyone not allowed in a holy role, here anyone not a priest, even a Levite.
b: A zar is an "outsider" in a given setting: here, anyone not descended from Aaron, including other Levites like Korah. The word is used for "strange fire" (Leviticus 10:1) and for laypeople who come too near (3:10, 38; 18:4, 7). Uzziah later learned the lesson when he entered the temple to burn incense (2 Chronicles 26:18: "Uzziah, it is not your place to burn incense to the LORD. That belongs to the priests, Aaron's descendants").

a: You have killed the LORD's people!
p: After everything, the whole community blames Moses and Aaron for the deaths.
b: This is the bitter turn of the chapter. The people saw the earth swallow the rebels and fire consume the 250, and yet the next day they accuse Moses and Aaron of murder. They call the dead "the LORD's people," taking the rebels' side. Ramban says they thought Moses had chosen the fire-pan test knowing it would kill the 250. The story shows how hard it is to change a crowd's mind with signs alone (compare Luke 16:31).

a: He stood between the dead and the living
t: Between the dead and the living
p: Aaron, the priest the rebels attacked, runs into the plague and stops it: a picture of a mediator.
b: The high priest, holding the incense that killed the 250, now uses it to save the people who accused him. The incense becomes a shield. The Talmud says the angel of death himself had taught Moses this secret (Shabbat 89a). Wisdom of Solomon 18:20–25 retells the scene: "a blameless man" stood with prayer and incense "and blocked the wrath's way to the living." Many Christian readers see Christ the high priest who "always lives to plead for them" (Hebrews 7:25), standing between death and life.
r: Wisdom of Solomon 18:20–25; Hebrews 7:25; 1 Timothy 2:5; Exodus 32:30–32; Psalm 106:30

a: fourteen thousand seven hundred
p: The number is large, but small next to the six hundred thousand men of the census.
b: Those who take the numbers at face value note that 14,700 is about 2.5 percent of the fighting men counted in 1:46. Those who read elef as a clan or unit read it as fourteen units and seven hundred men (see 1:46). Either way, the verse makes the point that Korah's rebellion did not end with Korah: it spread to the whole people, and only Aaron's intercession stopped the death.

a: a staff for each father's house
p: The Hebrew matteh means both "staff" and "tribe." Each tribe's staff stands for the tribe itself.
b: Matteh is a walking stick or rod of office, and it is also the usual word in Numbers for a "tribe" (1:4, 16; 13:2), perhaps because each tribe's leader carried a staff as a sign of his rule. The test is a pun made solid: twelve staffs for twelve tribes, each with its leader's name, and Levi's with Aaron's name. A dead stick that comes to life will show which tribe God has chosen for the priesthood. The English and Hebrew verse numbers differ from here on: 16:36–50 is 17:1–15 in Hebrew Bibles, and 17:1–13 is 17:16–28.

a: in front of the testimony
p: "The testimony" means the tablets of the covenant kept in the ark, and so the ark itself.
b: The "testimony" (edut) is the stone tablets of the Ten Words, placed in the ark (Exodus 25:16, 21; 31:18). The tent is therefore called "the tent of the testimony" (17:7–8; 9:15). The staffs are laid before the most holy object in Israel, where God meets Moses (Exodus 25:22: "There I will meet you"). The test happens in God's presence, not by human vote.

a: there was the staff of Aaron
p: Jewish legend traced the staff to creation. Christians saw in the blooming wood a sign of Mary and the resurrection.
b: Later Jewish tradition gave the staff a long story: created on the eve of the first Sabbath (Mishnah Avot 5:6 lists "the staff" among things made then), passed from Adam down to Moses (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 40), and kept to return in the days of the Messiah (Numbers Rabbah 18:23). Psalm 110:2, "From Zion the LORD will send out the scepter of your strength," was read with it, since the word for scepter there, matteh, is the word for Aaron's staff. Early Christians read the dry staff that blossomed as a sign of the virgin birth and of Christ's resurrection. The second-century Protoevangelium of James tells of Joseph chosen as Mary's husband by a sign from his rod, a story that later artists showed as a rod in bloom.

a: ripened almonds
p: In one night the dead stick buds, blooms and bears almonds. "Almond" sounds like "watcher" in Hebrew.
b: The staff goes through the whole life of a plant overnight: buds, flowers and fruit. The almond (shaqed) is the first tree to bloom in Israel's late winter, and its name sounds like shoqed, "watching": God shows Jeremiah an almond branch and says, "I am watching over my word to do it" (Jeremiah 1:11–12). The lampstand in the holy place had cups shaped like almond flowers (Exodus 25:33–34), so the staff may recall the light of God's presence. Hebrews 9:4 says the ark held the jar of manna, Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets, though 1 Kings 8:9 says only the tablets were in it in Solomon's day.

a: a sign for the rebels
p: The Hebrew is "sons of rebellion," a phrase that returns at Meribah: "Listen, you rebels!"
b: "Rebels" here is bene meri, "sons of rebellion." The same root returns at the rock, where Moses shouts, "Listen, please, you rebels!" (20:10), using hammorim, and God says Moses and Aaron "rebelled" against his word (20:24). The staff is a lasting warning in the sanctuary. Ezekiel calls Israel "a house of rebellion" (bet meri) again and again (Ezekiel 2:5–8).

a: Look, we are dying!
p: Now the people swing from defiance to terror. Chapter 18 answers their question.
b: After the earth swallowing, the fire and the plague, the people finally fear the sanctuary, but now they think anyone who comes near will die. Their cry piles up three verbs of dying: "we are dying," "we perish," "we all perish." The next chapter answers: God appoints the priests and Levites to guard the sanctuary and to "bear the guilt" for any trespass (18:1–7), so that "there will be no more wrath on the Israelites" (18:5). Rashi and Milgrom both read chapter 18 as the direct answer to 17:12–13.

a: will bear the guilt of the sanctuary
t: Bearing the guilt of the sanctuary
p: The priests and Levites become the sanctuary's guards and take the blame if anyone trespasses.
b: "Bear the guilt" (nasa avon) here means to be held responsible and take the penalty. Jacob Milgrom argued that the priests and Levites served as a protective cordon, "lightning rods," around the sanctuary: if an Israelite encroached, the guards, not the whole people, would answer for it. Aaron and his sons answer for the holy things inside; the Levites guard the tent from outside (18:3–4). The arrangement answers the panic of 17:12–13.

a: They will be joined to you
p: "Be joined" is a play on the name Levi. Leah named him hoping her husband would join himself to her.
b: The verb yillavu, "they will be joined," sounds like Levi. When Leah named her third son, she said, "This time, now, my husband will join himself to me" (Genesis 29:34). Numbers plays on the name twice (18:2, 4): the Levites are "joined" to Aaron to serve. Jacob's blessing had a darker word for Levi (Genesis 49:5–7), but by now the tribe has been set apart for the sanctuary (3:5–13; 8:5–22).

a: I give you your priesthood as a gift of service
p: The priesthood is not a privilege seized, as Korah tried, but a gift God gives.
b: The verse answers Korah's demand (16:10): the priesthood cannot be taken, only given. Hebrews makes the same point: "No one takes the honor on his own; he must be called by God, as Aaron also was" (Hebrews 5:4). Many Christians, especially in Catholic and Orthodox churches, see their ordained ministry as a gift and calling in the same way; many Protestants stress the priesthood of all believers (1 Peter 2:9) while still seeing leadership as God's call. Jewish tradition holds that kohanim, priests by descent, keep their special status today.

a: Everything devoted in Israel will be yours
p: Cherem is something given wholly to God, never to be used or bought back. It returns in 21:2–3.
b: Cherem means something set apart for God completely and permanently. Leviticus 27:28 says no devoted thing may be sold or bought back; "it is most holy to the LORD." When it is property, it goes to the priests, as here and in Ezekiel 44:29. In war the same word means "devoted to destruction": people and things given to God by being destroyed (21:2–3; Deuteronomy 7:2; Joshua 6:17–19). The two meanings share one idea: nothing devoted may be kept for ordinary use.

a: five shekels of silver by the shekel of the holy place
p: Jews still perform the pidyon haben, the redemption of a firstborn son, with five silver coins.
b: Every firstborn belongs to God (Exodus 13:2), but human firstborns must be bought back. The price is five shekels, about 2 ounces of silver, paid when the child is a month old. Jewish families still hold a ceremony called pidyon haben on the 31st day after the birth of a firstborn son who is not from a priestly or Levite family: the father gives five silver coins to a kohen (Mishnah Bekhorot 8). Luke 2:22–24 tells how Mary and Joseph presented Jesus, a firstborn, at the temple.

a: a covenant of salt for all time
p: Salt does not spoil. To share salt was to bind a lasting agreement.
b: Salt preserves food and does not decay, so a "covenant of salt" is one that lasts. Every grain offering was to be salted with "the salt of your God's covenant" (Leviticus 2:13). David's kingship is a covenant of salt in 2 Chronicles 13:5. In the ancient Near East, eating salt together sealed a bond; officials in Ezra 4:14 say they "eat the salt of the palace," that is, they owe the king loyalty. Jesus tells his followers, "Keep salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another" (Mark 9:50).

a: I am your portion and your inheritance
p: The priests get no land. God himself is their share. Psalm writers took this as a prayer for all believers.
b: Each tribe gets land, but Aaron's house gets none: "I am your portion." Deuteronomy 10:9 and 18:1–2 say the same of the Levites, and Ezekiel 44:28 of the priests of the new temple. The psalmists borrowed the word, cheleq, for any devoted person: "The LORD is the share I was given, and my cup" (Psalm 16:5); "The rock of my heart, and my share, is God forever" (Psalm 73:26); compare Lamentations 3:24. In Christian thought, "clergy" comes from the Greek klēros, "lot, portion," though the link with this verse is debated.
r: Deuteronomy 10:9; Deuteronomy 18:1–2; Joshua 13:33; Ezekiel 44:28; Psalm 16:5; Psalm 73:26; Lamentations 3:24

a: I give every tithe in Israel as an inheritance
p: Here the tithe goes to the Levites; in Deuteronomy the farmer eats it. The rabbis counted several tithes.
