b: Numbers gives the whole tithe of Israel's produce to the Levites as wages. Deuteronomy 14:22–29 says the family eats the tithe at the central sanctuary, and every third year gives it to the Levite, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow. The rabbis harmonized by counting several tithes: a "first tithe" for the Levites (this passage), a "second tithe" eaten in Jerusalem, and a "poor tithe" in the third and sixth years; Tobit 1:7–8 already knows this system. Source critics see different stages of Israel's law. Hebrews 7:5 recalls that the Levites "take a tenth from the people."
r: Deuteronomy 14:22–29; Deuteronomy 26:12–15; Leviticus 27:30–33; Tobit 1:6–8; Nehemiah 10:37–39; Hebrews 7:5

a: they will bear their guilt
p: "Their guilt" could be the Levites' own, or the people's. Most think the Levites take the people's guilt for trespass.
b: The pronoun is unclear. If "their" means the Levites, the verse says they answer for their own failures as guards. If it means the Israelites, it says the Levites bear the people's guilt when an Israelite comes too near (18:22). Milgrom and many others take the second view: this is the point of the whole chapter, an answer to 17:12–13. The Targums and Rashi read it as the Levites bearing the Israelites' sins.

a: a tenth of the tithe
p: The Levites must give a tenth of what they receive to the priests. Nehemiah renews the rule after the exile.
b: The Levites are not exempt from giving. From the tithe they receive, they give a tenth, the best part, to Aaron's line. The rabbis called it terumat ma'aser, "the gift from the tithe." Nehemiah 10:38 renews it: "The Levites are to carry up a tenth of the tithe to our God's house." In Jewish practice the farmer separates it today, and since the priests cannot eat it in purity, it is set aside and not eaten.

a: This is the rule of the law
p: The rabbis made the red heifer their chief example of a chok, a decree obeyed without a reason given.
b: Jewish tradition divides commands into mishpatim, whose reasons people can see, and chuqqim, "statutes" or decrees kept because God commanded them. The red heifer is the classic chok. Rashi says the nations mock Israel about it, so the Torah calls it a statute: "I have decreed it; you may not question it." A midrash says even Solomon, wisest of men, could not understand it (Numbers Rabbah 19:3, on Ecclesiastes 7:23). When a pagan asked Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai about it, he gave a practical answer, then told his students: "The dead do not make unclean, nor does water make clean. It is the King's decree" (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 4:7; Numbers Rabbah 19:8).

a: a red heifer, flawless, with no defect in it
p: The Mishnah says only nine were ever burned. In recent years some groups have raised red heifers for a rebuilt temple.
b: The animal is a young cow (parah), "red" (adummah), probably reddish-brown, and "flawless" (temimah). The rabbis read "flawless" as "wholly red": two black or white hairs make it unfit (Mishnah Parah 2:5). Tractate Parah says only seven or nine were prepared from Moses to the destruction of the Second Temple (Parah 3:5), and Maimonides wrote that the tenth will be prepared by the Messiah. Its ashes were needed for priests to be pure for temple service. In 2022 a group linked with the Temple Institute brought red heifers from Texas to Israel, stirring hopes and alarm about rebuilding the temple.

a: outside the camp
p: The heifer dies outside the camp. Hebrews links the red heifer and the place "outside the gate" to Jesus.
b: Unlike most sacrifices, this one is killed and burned outside the camp, away from the altar. Hebrews draws on this rite twice. Hebrews 9:13–14: "if the blood of goats and bulls, and a heifer's ashes sprinkled on the defiled, make them holy so that their flesh is pure, how much more will the blood of Christ... purify our conscience from dead works." Hebrews 13:11–13 adds that Jesus "suffered outside the gate," so "let us go out to him outside the camp, carrying his disgrace." The church fathers, beginning with the Epistle of Barnabas 8, read the heifer as a figure of Christ. In Second Temple times it was burned on the Mount of Olives, facing the temple (Mishnah Parah 3:6–7).

a: along with its dung
t: A rite from the ancient world
p: Ancient peoples used ash, red wool and cedar to purify. The red heifer shares the materials, not the magic.
b: Rituals using cedar, red wool and burned materials to remove impurity are known from the Hittites and Mesopotamia, and Milgrom thought the red heifer rite was very old, once perhaps a magical rite against the dead, reshaped by Israel's priests. In Israel's version the ashes are a "sin offering" under the priests' control, there are no spells, and the dead have no power to harm. Some critics see the burning of the whole cow, even its dung, as a sign of the rite's archaic origin. The parallels show a shared ancient way of thinking about purity, not borrowing of a specific text.

a: cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn
p: The same three things are used to cleanse a person healed of skin disease. Hyssop returns at the cross.
b: Cedar wood, scarlet yarn and hyssop are also used to cleanse a person healed of skin disease (Leviticus 14:4–6, 49–52). Their red color may stand for blood and life, and cedar resists decay. Hyssop was a small plant, probably a kind of marjoram, whose leafy branches were good for sprinkling (Exodus 12:22). David prays, "Take away my sin with hyssop, and I will be pure" (Psalm 51:7). At the cross a sponge of sour wine is lifted to Jesus "on a hyssop branch" (John 19:29), and Hebrews 9:19 recalls Moses using scarlet wool and hyssop.

a: the priest will be unclean until evening
t: Makes the unclean clean, the clean unclean
p: Its handlers become unclean, yet its ashes make the unclean clean. The rabbis called it a great paradox.
b: The priest, the man who burns the heifer, and the man who gathers the ashes all become unclean (19:7–10), and so does the one who sprinkles the water (19:21). Yet the same water cleanses a person defiled by a corpse. A saying in the midrash puts it this way: the red heifer "purifies the impure and makes impure the pure" (Numbers Rabbah 19). Milgrom's explanation is often followed: the heifer is a purification offering (19:9) whose ashes act like a cleaning agent. They draw impurity out of the defiled person, and so they leave impurity on everyone who handles them, like a sponge that gets dirty as it cleans.

a: the water for impurity
p: Mei niddah is water that removes impurity. The Greek called it "water of sprinkling."
b: Mei niddah literally means "water of impurity" or "water of separation" (KJV "water of separation"). Niddah is the word for impurity, especially menstrual impurity (Leviticus 15:19), so the phrase means water that deals with impurity, as "sin offering" deals with sin. The Septuagint calls it "water of sprinkling" (hydōr rhantismou). Hebrews speaks of "the blood of sprinkling" of Jesus (Hebrews 12:24) and of hearts "sprinkled clean" (Hebrews 10:22). Ezekiel 36:25 promises, "I will sprinkle pure water over you, and you will be clean."
r: Leviticus 15:19; Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1; Hebrews 10:22; Hebrews 12:24; 1 Peter 1:2

a: It is a sin offering
p: The Hebrew hatta't can mean "sin offering" or "purification offering." Here it cleanses impurity, not moral sin.
b: The usual translation of hatta't is "sin offering," kept here to match Leviticus. Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, argue it is better called a "purification offering," because it often cleanses things that are not sins at all: childbirth (Leviticus 12:6–8), skin disease (Leviticus 14:19), and here contact with a corpse. Its blood (or here its ash) purges impurity from the sanctuary or the person. The related verb in 19:12, 19 means "to purify" or "to free from sin."

a: Whoever touches a dead body
p: Corpse impurity was the strongest kind. Scholars connect it with the gap between death and the living God.
b: Of all kinds of uncleanness, a corpse's is the strongest: it lasts seven days, spreads through a tent (19:14), and needs this special water. Milgrom argued that the purity laws as a whole oppose death: skin disease, loss of blood or semen, and corpses all stand for death, while the holy God is the source of life. Mary Douglas stressed the system's order and wholeness. Uncleanness is not sin; burying the dead was a duty. Priests had to avoid corpses except for close family (Leviticus 21:1–4). The priest and Levite in Jesus' parable who pass by may be avoiding corpse impurity (Luke 10:31–32), and Jesus touches the dead to raise them (Luke 7:14; Mark 5:41).

a: when a person dies in a tent
p: Uncleanness spreads to everyone under the same roof as a corpse. A whole tractate of the Mishnah works out the rule.
b: Uncleanness from a corpse fills the whole tent and every open container in it (19:15). The rabbis extended this to any roofed space and wrote a whole tractate, Ohalot ("Tents"), on how it spreads. Because of these laws, Jews of priestly descent (kohanim) still avoid cemeteries and the same building as a dead body, except for close relatives. Since no red heifer ashes exist today, Jewish law treats everyone as unclean from corpse contact, which is one reason many rabbis forbid walking on the Temple Mount.

a: running water
p: The Hebrew is "living water," water from a spring or stream. Jesus offers living water in John.
b: Mayim chayyim, literally "living water," means fresh, flowing water from a spring or stream, not water stored in a cistern (Genesis 26:19; Leviticus 14:5). Jeremiah calls God "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13), and Zechariah 14:8 sees living water flowing from Jerusalem. Jesus offers the Samaritan woman "living water" (John 4:10), with a play on both meanings, and speaks of rivers of living water flowing from the believer (John 7:38–39).
r: Genesis 26:19; Leviticus 14:5; Jeremiah 2:13; Zechariah 14:8; John 4:10–14; John 7:38–39

a: he will free him from sin
p: The verb chitte' means to remove sin or impurity. David uses it in Psalm 51: "purge me with hyssop."
b: The Hebrew verb chitte' is a form of the word for sin, chata', but it means the opposite: to take sin or impurity away, to "de-sin." The person sprinkled on the seventh day is set free from impurity. Psalm 51:7 uses the same verb with the same plant: "Take away my sin (techatte'eni) with hyssop, and I will be pure." David borrows the language of the red heifer rite to ask for moral cleansing.

a: he has made the LORD's sanctuary unclean
p: A person who stays unclean pollutes the sanctuary from a distance. This is why the rite matters for the whole people.
b: Milgrom argued that in priestly thought, impurity is like a polluting force that reaches God's sanctuary even from a distance. If too much builds up, God may leave his house (Ezekiel 8–11). That is why refusing purification is so serious that the person is "cut off" (see 15:30). The rite guards the whole community, not just the individual. Others think the verse means only that the unclean person might enter the sanctuary and defile it directly.

a: in the first month
p: No year is given. Comparing 33:38, this is the fortieth year. Almost four decades pass without a word.
b: The text gives the month but not the year. Aaron dies on Mount Hor in the fifth month of the fortieth year (33:38), so most readers, with Rashi, place this in the first month of the fortieth year. If so, the thirty-eight years of wandering between chapters 14 and 20 pass in silence; only the laws of 15–19 and the stops listed in 33:19–36 fill the gap. The generation that left Egypt has died, and the people at Kadesh are mostly their children. Some scholars think the story originally followed the second year directly.

a: Miriam died there and was buried there
p: Right after Miriam dies, the water runs out. Jewish tradition says a well followed Israel in her honor.
b: The text says only that Miriam died and "there was no water for the community" (20:2). The rabbis connected the two: God gave Israel three gifts for the sake of three leaders: the well for Miriam, the cloud for Aaron, and the manna for Moses; when Miriam died, the well dried up (Taanit 9a). An older legend says a rock-well traveled with Israel through the desert (Tosefta Sukkah 3:11; Pseudo-Philo, Biblical Antiquities 10:7). Paul may know this story when he writes of "the spiritual rock that went along with them; and that rock was Christ" (1 Corinthians 10:4). Some Jewish families now set a "cup of Miriam" with water at the Passover table.

a: Speak to the rock before their eyes
p: In Exodus 17 Moses strikes a rock. Here he is told to speak to it. Readers see one event told twice, or two events.
b: Exodus 17:1–7 tells of water from a rock at Horeb, at a place called "Massah and Meribah," early in the journey. There God commands, "You will hit the rock." This story is set at Kadesh near the end, but it is also called Meribah (20:13), and here God says "speak." Traditional readers see two events, forty years apart, with a test of whether Moses would trust God's word rather than repeat the old method. Many critical scholars see two versions of one tradition about a quarrel over water, an older one in Exodus and a Priestly one here.

a: Listen, please, you rebels!
p: Psalm 106 says Moses' sin was in what he said: "he let careless words slip from his lips."
b: Psalm 106:32–33 retells the scene: "At the waters of Meribah they stirred up his anger, / and Moses came to harm on their account, / for they defied his spirit, / and he let careless words slip from his lips." The word "rebels" (hammorim) is the same root as the "sons of rebellion" for whom Aaron's staff was kept (17:10). The staff Moses takes "from before the LORD" (20:9) may be that very staff of Aaron. Moses calls the people rebels, and God then says it is Moses and Aaron who rebelled (20:24; 27:14).

a: You did not believe me, to treat me as holy in the Israelites' eyes
p: The text never says plainly. Jewish and Christian readers have given at least seven answers.
b: S. D. Luzzatto remarked that interpreters had loaded Moses with many sins where the text names one. (1) He struck the rock instead of speaking to it (Rashi). (2) He lost his temper and called the people "rebels" (Maimonides, Eight Chapters 4). (3) He said "Are we to bring water," as if the power were his (Ramban, following Rabbenu Chananel). (4) Unbelief, the fault God names: "you did not believe me" (Calvin; Keil and Delitzsch). (5) He should have worked the miracle by his own word (Joseph Albo). (6) The real causes were earlier failures, the scouts for Moses and the calf for Aaron, and Meribah was only the occasion (Abravanel). (7) Deuteronomy blames the people: "because of you" (Deuteronomy 1:37; 3:26). Critical scholars think a Priestly writer left the fault vague out of respect. Many Christians add a typology: the rock is Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4), struck once for all.
r: Deuteronomy 1:37; Deuteronomy 3:23–27; Deuteronomy 32:50–52; Psalm 106:32–33; 1 Corinthians 10:4; Hebrews 4:8

a: the waters of Meribah
p: Meribah means "quarrel." Kadesh means "holy." The verse plays on both names.
b: The people "quarreled" (rav) with the LORD, so the place is Meribah, "quarrel." God "showed himself holy" (yiqqadesh) at Kadesh, "holy place." The failure was that Moses and Aaron did not "treat me as holy" (lehaqdisheni, 20:12). Later texts call it "Meribath-kadesh" (27:14; Deuteronomy 32:51) to tell it apart from the Meribah of Exodus 17:7. In the end God shows his holiness anyway, by giving water and by judging his own leaders.

a: Your brother Israel
p: Israel approaches Edom as a brother, recalling Jacob and Esau. Edom refuses, and the bitterness lasts for centuries.
b: Edom descends from Esau, Jacob's twin (Genesis 25:30; 36:1). Moses' message is polite and family-minded, like Jacob's careful message to Esau in Genesis 32:3–5. Edom answers with the sword. Deuteronomy 23:7 still says, "Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother," and Deuteronomy 2:4–8 tells the story more gently, saying Israel passed by Edom without fighting. Later prophets condemn Edom for its "violence against your brother Jacob" (Obadiah 10–12; Amos 1:11).
r: Genesis 25:23–30; Genesis 32:3–5; Genesis 33:1–16; Deuteronomy 2:1–8; Deuteronomy 23:7; Obadiah 10–12; Amos 1:11; Judges 11:17

a: He sent an angel
p: The Hebrew mal'akh means both. Rashi says the "messenger" was Moses.
b: Mal'akh is the same word used in 20:14 for Moses' "messengers" to Edom. Most take it here as the angel who went before Israel (Exodus 14:19; 23:20: "I am sending an angel in front of you"). Rashi and some others say it means Moses himself, God's messenger, since prophets are called messengers (Haggai 1:13; 2 Chronicles 36:15–16). Either way, Israel tells Edom that the God who heard their cry led them out.

a: the King's Highway
p: An old north-south road along the plateau east of the Dead Sea, from the Gulf of Aqaba to Damascus.
b: The King's Highway ran along the high plateau east of the Jordan Valley and the Arabah, through Edom, Moab and Ammon, linking the Gulf of Aqaba with Damascus. Much of it was later paved as the Roman Via Nova Traiana (AD 111–114), after Rome annexed the region in AD 106, and a modern road still follows it. Archaeologists debate when Edom became a kingdom able to block the road: surveys once found little settlement there before the 8th century BC, but excavations at copper sites in the Arabah, such as Khirbat en-Nahas, show organized industry by the 10th century BC or earlier.

a: Mount Hor
p: Tradition since Josephus places it near Petra. Many modern scholars look nearer Kadesh.
b: Mount Hor is "on the border of the land of Edom" (20:23). Josephus placed Aaron's death on a high mountain near Petra (Antiquities 4.82–83), and the peak called Jebel Harun ("Aaron's mountain"), with a small shrine on top, still carries the tradition. That is far from Kadesh, and it lies inside Edom. Many modern scholars prefer a hill northeast of Kadesh, such as Jebel Madurah. Deuteronomy 10:6 places Aaron's death at Moserah, another unknown site, which may be near Mount Hor or reflect a different tradition.

a: Strip Aaron of his garments and put them on his son Eleazar
p: The high priest's office passes to his son by passing on his clothes, while Aaron is still alive.
b: The high priest's garments were the sign of his office (Exodus 28–29). Exodus 29:29 says, "Aaron's holy clothes will go to his sons after him." Moses takes them off Aaron and puts them on Eleazar before Aaron dies, so there is no gap in the priesthood. Aaron's death is quiet and dignified: no complaint is recorded. Here the Hebrew says only that Aaron "will be gathered"; 20:24 has the full phrase, "gathered to his people." Elijah's mantle passing to Elisha (2 Kings 2:13–14) is a similar handover. Aaron dies at 123, on the first day of the fifth month (33:38–39).

a: all the house of Israel wept for Aaron thirty days
p: The rabbis said all Israel, men and women, mourned Aaron because he was a peacemaker.
b: "All the house of Israel" mourned Aaron, as they would later mourn Moses for thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8). Rashi notes that for Moses the text says "the Israelites" wept, but for Aaron "all the house of Israel," men and women alike, because Aaron made peace between quarreling friends and between husbands and wives (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 12). Hillel taught, "Be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace" (Mishnah Avot 1:12). Thirty days of mourning (sheloshim) is still Jewish custom.

a: The Canaanite king of Arad
p: Tel Arad has a famous Israelite fortress and shrine, but no city from the time of the exodus.
b: Tel Arad in the eastern Negev was a large city in the Early Bronze Age (about 3000–2650 BC) and an Israelite fortress from about the 10th to the 6th century BC, with a small shrine to the LORD inside. Excavators found no Late Bronze Age settlement, when most date the exodus. Some say the "Arad" here was a region or another town, perhaps Tel Malhata nearby; others think the story reflects later conditions. "Atharim" is unknown; the Targums and KJV read it as "the spies" (see the variant).

a: I will devote their towns to destruction
p: In war, cherem meant giving a city to God by destroying it. Readers answer the moral problem differently.
b: The verb hecherim means to devote something wholly to God (see 18:14), here by destroying it, so that nothing is taken as plunder. Israel was not alone: the Moabite king Mesha boasts on his stone inscription (about 840 BC) that he took Nebo and "devoted" its seven thousand people to his god Ashtar-Chemosh. Jewish and Christian readers have handled these texts in different ways: as unique commands for one time and place; as ancient war rhetoric that exaggerates; as a ban on profiting from war; or as texts to be read in light of later teaching on mercy. Here Israel makes the vow itself, and God accepts it.

a: the people's patience grew short
p: The Hebrew says "the soul of the people became short," an idiom for losing patience.
b: Vattiqtsar nefesh ha'am means literally "the soul (or breath) of the people grew short." It describes being worn out and impatient, as when Samson's "soul was short to death" from Delilah's nagging (Judges 16:16), or when God's "soul grew short" over Israel's misery (Judges 10:16). After another long detour around Edom, the people are at the end of their patience. The opposite is being "long of anger," slow to anger, as God is (14:18).

a: this flimsy food
p: The Hebrew word suggests something light and worthless. The rabbis said manna was so pure it left no waste.
b: The people mean the manna. The word qeloqel appears only here and comes from a root meaning "light, slight": food with no weight to it, "wretched" or "miserable." The KJV has "this light bread." The Talmud took "light" in a different sense: manna was absorbed completely into the body, leaving no waste, and the people complained that such food must swell their bellies (Yoma 75b). Psalm 78:25 calls the same food "the bread of angels." Notice the contradiction in the complaint: "There is no bread," and "we are sick of this food."

a: the burning snakes
p: The snakes are seraphim, "burning ones," the same word as the seraphs Isaiah saw around God's throne.
b: Hannechashim hasserafim is "the snakes, the burning ones." The name may come from the burning pain of their bite, or from their fiery color. Deuteronomy 8:15 recalls "the huge and fearsome wilderness, with its burning snakes and scorpions." Isaiah 14:29 and 30:6 speak of a "flying seraph" in the desert. In Isaiah 6:2 the seraphim are winged beings around God's throne. Egyptian art often shows the uraeus, a rearing cobra, sometimes with wings, as a protector of kings and gods, and Herodotus (2.75) reports stories of winged snakes in Arabia. Many scholars think the images are connected.

a: We have sinned
p: For once the people confess and ask Moses to pray. God answers, but does not remove the snakes.
b: In chapters 11–20 the people complain and Moses intercedes without being asked. Here they confess ("we have sinned") and ask him to pray, and he does. God does not take the snakes away. He gives a way to live through the bite. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, see a lesson: healing comes by looking to what God provides, while the danger is still present. Paul warns, "Let us not test Christ, as some of them tested him and were killed by the snakes" (1 Corinthians 10:9).

a: Make yourself a burning one and put it on a pole
p: Jewish tradition insists the image did not heal by itself. Looking up turned the heart to God.
b: Making an image of a snake seems to clash with the command against images (Exodus 20:4). The Mishnah asks, "Could a snake kill or give life? No: when Israel looked upward and set their hearts on their Father in heaven, they were healed" (Rosh Hashanah 3:8). Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–7 says the same: "the one who turned to it was saved not by the thing he looked at, but by you, the Savior of all." Targum Pseudo-Jonathan adds that the one bitten lived "if he directed his heart to the name of the word of the LORD." The "pole" (nes) is a standard or banner raised high to be seen.
r: Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 3:8; Wisdom of Solomon 16:5–12; Exodus 17:15; Isaiah 11:10–12; Isaiah 45:22

a: So Moses made a snake of bronze
p: A copper snake was found in a Midianite desert shrine at Timna. It shows such objects existed, nothing more.
b: At Timna, an ancient copper-mining valley north of Eilat, the archaeologist Beno Rothenberg excavated in 1969 a small Egyptian shrine to the goddess Hathor, used from about the late 14th to the mid-12th century BC. In a later phase, in the later 12th century, apparently under Midianites, the shrine was remade as a tent shrine, and in it lay a copper snake about 5 inches long with a gilded head. Snakes were linked with healing and life across the ancient world, from Egyptian and Canaanite amulets to the Greek healer Asclepius, whose staff has a snake. Many scholars think Israel's Nehushtan came out of this world, perhaps through Moses' Midianite in-laws. The link is possible but not proven.

a: a snake of bronze
p: In Hebrew, "snake" is nachash and "bronze" is nechoshet. The bronze snake is a word play made in metal.
b: God told Moses to make a "burning one" (saraf); Moses makes a nechash nechoshet, a "snake of bronze," two words that sound alike. Bronze, or copper, also has a reddish, fiery shine. The object was kept for centuries. King Hezekiah, about 715 BC, "crushed to pieces the bronze snake Moses had made, because up to those days the Israelites had been burning incense to it. People called it Nehushtan" (2 Kings 18:4). What God gave for healing had become an idol.

a: he would look at the bronze snake and live
p: Jesus compares his own death to the bronze snake lifted up in the wilderness.
b: In John 3:14–15 Jesus says, "In the same way that Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, the Son of Man has to be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him will have eternal life." John uses "lifted up" for the cross (John 8:28; 12:32–33). The likeness lies in the lifting, the looking, and life for those dying from a bite. The Epistle of Barnabas (12:5–7) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue 94, 112) develop the comparison. Luther and Calvin both preached on it. Some modern readers note the reversal: the image of what was killing them becomes the means of healing, as Paul says Christ "became a curse for us" (Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21).
r: John 3:14–15; John 8:28; John 12:32–33; Galatians 3:13; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Isaiah 45:22

a: the Valley of Zered
p: Two great canyons cut the plateau east of the Dead Sea and marked the borders of Edom, Moab and the Amorites.
b: The Zered is probably the Wadi al-Hasa, which runs into the southern end of the Dead Sea and was the border between Edom and Moab. The Arnon is the Wadi Mujib, a deep gorge midway along the Dead Sea, often named as Moab's northern border (21:13, 26). Deuteronomy 2:13–14 says crossing the Zered marked the end of the thirty-eight years. The route in 21:10–20 does not fully match the list in 33:41–49; it may combine different traditions or different parts of the journey.

a: the Book of the Wars of the LORD
p: Numbers quotes a lost book of war songs. Its two lines are among the hardest in the Bible to translate.
b: This lost collection is cited only here. It was probably a book of poems about the LORD's battles, like the Book of Jashar (Joshua 10:13). Its quote is a fragment. "Waheb in Suphah" may be two place names. The Targums and Rashi read vahev as "what he gave" and Suphah as the Sea of Reeds. The Septuagint reads, "Therefore it is said in a book, 'The war of the Lord set Zoob on fire,'" taking Waheb as a name and finding a verb "burn." Duane Christensen reconstructed "He came in a storm," and many follow him. The Talmud tells a legend that at the Arnon the cliffs closed on Amorites hiding in the canyon walls (Berakhot 54a–b). Critical scholars cite the verse as evidence that the Torah's writers used older sources; traditional readers can agree, since Moses could quote earlier songs.

a: Spring up, well!
p: A short work song for digging a well. The Dead Sea Scrolls read the well as the Torah.
b: This little song is like a work chant sung while digging for water in a dry riverbed. Rabbinic tradition linked it with Miriam's well (see 20:1). The Damascus Document from Qumran (CD VI, 3–11) reads it as an allegory: "the well is the Law, and those who dug it are the converts of Israel," and the "scepter" (mechoqeq, also "lawgiver") is "the interpreter of the Law." Jesus' words to the woman at Jacob's well about "a spring inside him, of water leaping up into eternal life" (John 4:14) are read by some as an echo.

a: with a scepter
p: Mechoqeq is a ruler's staff, but the word can also mean "lawgiver."
b: Mechoqeq comes from chaqaq, "to engrave, decree." It can mean a ruler's staff (Genesis 49:10, "the ruler's staff from between his feet") or a person who decrees, "lawgiver" (Isaiah 33:22; KJV here "by the direction of the lawgiver"). The princes dig, perhaps only symbolically, with their staffs of office. The Qumran reading of this verse turns the "lawgiver" into the community's teacher (see the note on 21:17).

a: Sihon king of the Amorites
p: The defeat of Sihon and Og became one of Israel's best-remembered victories, sung in the Psalms.
b: Sihon ruled from Heshbon over the land between the Arnon and the Jabbok; Og ruled Bashan to the north (21:33). Their defeat was Israel's first conquest of land, and it became a fixed part of Israel's memory: Deuteronomy 2:24–3:11, Joshua 2:10, Judges 11:19–22 (Jephthah's argument with Ammon), Nehemiah 9:22, and Psalms 135:11 and 136:19–20 ("Sihon king of the Amorites, for his loyal love lasts forever; and Og king of Bashan"). Outside the Bible neither king is known.
r: Deuteronomy 2:24–37; Deuteronomy 3:1–11; Joshua 2:10; Judges 11:19–26; Psalm 135:10–12; Psalm 136:17–22; Nehemiah 9:22

a: Heshbon was the city of Sihon
p: Excavations at Tell Hesban found no city from the Late Bronze Age. Scholars read the evidence in several ways.
b: Heshbon is identified with Tell Hesban in Jordan, which keeps the name. Excavations by Andrews University (1968–1976) found a village of Iron Age I, the 12th and 11th centuries BC, but no Late Bronze Age city. The Iron I finds suit scholars who date Israel's arrival around 1200 BC, though a village is small for a royal capital. Others suggest Sihon's Heshbon stood at another site, such as Tell Jalul. In a well-known exchange, John Van Seters argued that 21:21–35 was written late, from Deuteronomy 2 and Judges 11, and John Bartlett replied that it keeps an older tradition. Many critical scholars think the story reflects times when Heshbon was a real city, from Iron Age II on. The question feeds the wider debate over the date of the exodus.
r: Deuteronomy 2:24–30; Joshua 13:10, 17; Song of Songs 7:4; Isaiah 15:4; Jeremiah 48:2, 34

a: the singers of sayings
t: Whose song is the Song of Heshbon?
p: The poem may be an Amorite victory song over Moab that Israel took over, or an Israelite taunt.
b: The "singers of sayings" (moshelim) are people who recite meshalim, proverbs or taunt songs (compare Balaam's "sayings," 23:7). Two readings are common. (1) The poem is an Amorite song celebrating Sihon's victory over Moab (21:26), quoted to show Israel had rightly taken land that was already Amorite, not Moabite (compare Judges 11:15–26). (2) It is an Israelite taunt: "Come to Heshbon, let it be rebuilt!" mocks the ruined Amorite capital. Some think the poem is a much later song from Israel's wars with Moab in the 800s BC.

a: For fire went out from Heshbon
p: Jeremiah's oracle against Moab borrows several lines of this poem almost word for word.
b: Jeremiah 48:45–46 quotes the song: "Fire went out from Heshbon, a flame from the midst of Sihon... Woe to you, Moab! The people of Chemosh are lost, for your sons are taken off into captivity, and your daughters into captivity." Jeremiah turns an old song of Moab's defeat into a prophecy of Moab's fall in his own day. This shows the poem was known and treated as a classic.

a: people of Chemosh
p: Chemosh was the national god of Moab. The Mesha Stele names him often.
b: Chemosh (Kemosh) was Moab's chief god, as the LORD was Israel's (Judges 11:24; 1 Kings 11:7, 33). The Mesha Stele, a Moabite inscription of about 840 BC found at Dibon in 1868, says Moab was oppressed by Israel "because Chemosh was angry with his land," and that Chemosh later gave Mesha victory. It mentions Dibon, Medeba, Jahaz and Ataroth, places named in this chapter and in chapter 32. The poem pictures Chemosh as a god who let his own sons and daughters become refugees and captives.

a: Og king of Bashan
t: Og, the last of the Rephaim
p: Deuteronomy calls Og the last of the giant Rephaim. Ugaritic texts link his cities with the honored dead.
b: Deuteronomy 3:11 says Og was the last of the Rephaim, a race of giants, and his iron (or basalt) bed, nine cubits long (about 13 feet), could be seen in Rabbah. Og ruled from Ashtaroth and Edrei (Joshua 12:4). A Ugaritic text from about 1200 BC (KTU 1.108) names a god Rapiu who "sits in Ashtarot" and rules "in Edrei," and the rpum at Ugarit are the honored dead. Many scholars think Bashan was known as a land of the dead heroes, and the giant king grew out of that tradition. Later Jewish legend made Og survive the flood (Niddah 61a) and try to crush Israel with a mountain (Berakhot 54b).
r: Deuteronomy 3:1–11; Joshua 12:4; Joshua 13:12; Amos 2:9; Psalm 68:15–16; Isaiah 26:14

a: until no survivor was left to him
p: As with Sihon, the text says Og's people were all killed. The same hard questions apply as in 21:2.
b: Deuteronomy 3:6 says Israel "devoted them to destruction," men, women and children, as with Sihon (Deuteronomy 2:34). The phrase "no survivor was left" is a standard formula of ancient war reports, found also in Assyrian and Moabite inscriptions, and many scholars think it is partly stock language rather than a body count. See the note on 21:2 for how Jewish and Christian readers have dealt with such texts. With Sihon and Og defeated, Israel holds the land east of the Jordan, which Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh will ask for (32:33).
